en: The Avadāna of the Great Being, King Maṇicūḍa, the Bodhisattva.
Then King Aśoka, standing before him with palms joined in reverence, bowed to the Arhat Upagupta and again made this request: (1)
"Venerable sir, I wish to hear another well-spoken avadāna of the Blessed One, which he deems fit to instruct.
Having heard this request made by the king, that wise Arhat ascetic [replied]:
Having thus addressed King Aśoka, he commanded him:
"Listen well, O Great King, to that which was spoken by my teacher; I shall declare it to you exactly as it was told. Having heard it, rejoice with devotion."
Just as that great being, even after enjoying great bliss together with Brahmā in the Śubhakṛtsna heaven, did not rejoice there without giving; so too,
while staying there, that great being remained intensely devoted to the practice of generosity.
"What is the state of affairs in the world of men?"—having thus reflected, he looked out.
At that time, all human beings were indifferent toward truth and righteousness;
they were afflicted by envy and avarice, and intoxicated by pride and negligence.
Even the brahmins were of immoral conduct, having abandoned the traditions of their own lineage; they were wretched, addicted to evil deeds, and revilers of the true Dharma.
All the kings likewise, along with their ministers, servants, and citizens, were the same.
Blinded by the intoxication and pride of the afflictions, they practice the ten unwholesome deeds.
Thus, all those mortals who commit great transgressions will surely die tormented by the fire of the afflictions and go to hell. 9–10.
Since they lack any teacher whose nature is Dharma to show them the direction of their welfare and purpose,
all those deluded men wander even into sinful acts; therefore,
for their benefit, I shall descend from here to the surface of the earth.
Having obtained birth in a royal family of a king, may I become a sovereign;
there, having bestowed gifts upon all supplicants according to their desires, may I cause all sentient beings everywhere to abide in perfect restraint.
Then all those men, devoted to the qualities of truth and righteousness, having taken up the vow of the conduct of awakening, shall always move within the auspicious state.
Then, they of stainless conduct, with the three spheres completely purified—
May I become a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, a practitioner of the holy life (brahmacārin).
For this reason, having gone from here and taken birth upon the surface of the earth,
may I become the sovereign of all worlds and cause the world to practice what is auspicious.
Having meditated thus, that Bodhisattva, seeking the Dharma and eager for the bull,
then bowed with palms joined and, while looking on, made this announcement: "O God, wicked conduct has now been set in motion throughout the world."
Therefore, all those wicked men who are devoted to the ten unwholesome paths—
having gone to that world of mortals and becoming the sovereign of all worlds, I shall awaken all those men and cause them to practice the path of restraint.

"Therefore, may you graciously grant me permission; out of compassion, please be pleased with me so that, having taken up the vow of the conduct of awakening, I may proceed for the welfare of the world. Having heard this prayer made by him, Kāśyapa—
Having meditated for a long time, he, with a serene mind, urged him, saying, "Go. Then that Bodhisattva, having received that permission and being gladdened,
remained there and surveyed his pure place of birth upon the earth.

Then, in that world of men, there was the great city of Sāketa—prosperous, flourishing, ever-vigorous, well-supplied with food, and free from calamity; where the wicked conduct of the Kali age had been stilled, and where there were no riots, tumults, or thieves. (23)
Crowded with virtuous and wealthy people, it shone like a single fragment of heaven.
There, the sovereign king Brahmadatta, endowed with great prosperity,
protected all his subjects according to dharma as if they were his own children.
His chief queen was the lady Kāntimatī, who was like Rati;
she was pure in conduct, beautiful of limb, and followed the dharma of her husband.
When that queen was filled with passion, the king likewise became enamored.
Then that lord of kings enjoyed himself with her as he desired.
Having seen this, that Great Being, the Bodhisattva, descending from heaven,
arrived there and entered the womb of that queen in that auspicious place.
From the moment she became pregnant, Subhāṣiṇī desired to give to all seekers whatever they wished;
thereafter, that queen-mahiṣī became one who fulfilled the desires of all supplicants.
Having bowed at the lotus feet of her husband, she entreated him with great respect:
"O Lord, if you have compassion for me, grant me your permission so that I may fulfill whatever desire I have."

When the queen, his wife, had thus entreated him, that lord of men, looking upon his beloved with a smile, spoke to her as follows: "O lady, what is it that you desire? Everything you wish for shall be fulfilled."
"I shall fulfill it accordingly; tell me that truth before me.
When the Lord had thus commanded, the queen was filled with joy and, gazing upon her husband, the great king, spoke as follows.
"O Lord, standing upon a great heap of gold, I am able to give all of it as I desire to the ascetics, brahmins, and others.
Having heard what was thus declared by his wife, that lord of men—
Filled with wonder, he questioned the knower of omens, reporting this matter to him.
(36) Having heard what was reported and having carefully considered that omen, the wise knower of omens spoke thus before the king. (37)
"O King, know this: your wife is certainly pregnant;
this is surely the power of that which has entered her womb.
Indeed, this must be a Great Being, your wise son. (38)
"Therefore, be gracious, O Great King, so that there may be prosperity and well-being for you.
Having heard what was spoken by him, the king was filled with joy;
having honored that knower of omens, he desired to have it carried out.
Then that king, approaching his wife and seeking to appease her, commanded:
"Do everything exactly as you wish.
Having heard this command from her husband, the queen was filled with joy.
Having obtained the king's permission, she proceeded to act accordingly.
Then that queen, seated upon a great heap of gold,
gave as much gold as was desired to ascetics, brahmins, and supplicants.
Then that queen, having once again satisfied all the people with foods endowed with the six flavors, desired to see them.
Then, having informed the king, that queen was filled with great joy.
Having thus obtained permission from her lord, she began to look [upon him].
Then, having respectfully invited all the people,
she honored them and caused them to be satisfied with food of six flavors.
Seeing all those worlds— whether supplicants or even the wretched— content with food possessing the six flavors, she experienced great joy.
Then that virtuous queen sat upon a great lion-throne.

He desired to teach the True Dharma to all the worlds. (48) Having thus informed the King and received the Lord's permission, he then joyfully set out to teach the Dharma after summoning all the people. (49)
Then, having been questioned in that manner by the lord of men, those diviners, after deliberating, reported once more in the presence of the king:
"O Lord, a great being has entered the womb of your queen."
"Surely this is her power, that she should teach the Dharma.
Therefore, O King, let this queen—who seeks the welfare of all sentient beings—teach the True Dharma to all the worlds according to her wish. (51-52)
Having heard this instruction given by them, that lord of men was delighted; having quickly cleansed the palace, he adorned it beautifully.
Therein [he placed] a very large lion-throne, richly endowed with gold and jewels.
Having had it prepared, he adorned it with fine Chinese silks and white woolen cloths.
Then that king, the lord of men, having summoned all those people who were sounding the bells, addressed them while looking upon them as follows: (54–55)
"Sirs, since this queen desires to teach the Dharma,
summon all the people here with haste.
Having heard this command from the king, all those people—
Saying "So be it," they bowed to the king and joyfully set about doing as instructed.
Having rung the bell throughout that city,
they exhorted the people exactly as the lord of men had commanded.
"Listen, all you citizens, to this decree firmly ordered by the King:
the Queen, the chief consort, desires to instruct us in the Dharma.
Therefore, those who joyfully wish to hear this noble Dharma [are invited]. (59)
"Let all those who seek virtuous qualities assemble and listen.
Having heard this proclamation, all the citizens, filled with wonder, went joyfully to the royal palace to hear his teaching of the Dharma.
Then the radiant Queen, adorned with all her ornaments,
ascended the lion-throne and took her seat in the midst of the assembly.
Seeing that goddess, who was shining with splendor, those citizens were filled with joy.
Having bowed with reverence, gazing [at her] and placing her at their head, they took refuge in her. Then, while that body of people was seated all around,
Kāntimatī, having seen all those people, stood there composed in meditation.
Then, through the power of the Bodhisattva Sanmati, who was born from a womb, she taught these verses concerning the meaning of the True Dharma:
"One established in the Dharma proceeds with an increase in virtues. (65)
He attains supreme contentment and renown; when suffering arises, he does not fall into despair; and in the future life, he obtains auspicious happiness. 66
For Dharma indeed protects one endowed with Dharma, just as a father protects a son of noble conduct; therefore, the wise man, possessed of the power of knowledge, [should practice it].
As long as one may practice the Dharma from this [teaching],
the Dharma indeed protects the one endowed with Dharma, just as a royal umbrella provides shelter when it rains during the rainy season.
The Sugata has taught the benefits of the Dharma:
one who practices the Dharma does not go to an evil rebirth; but the man who practices non-Dharma is heedless.
Whichever state of existence a person of deluded view goes to, having destroyed the Dharma and lived according to it, he is bound, just as a black antelope is captured. 69
For non-dharma is not dharma;
both have equal ripening,
yet through non-dharma they go to hell.

Thinking, "Through the Dharma they go to a good rebirth," those who desire true happiness should always abandon what is not the Dharma; having heard the true Dharma with faith, they should practice excellent self-restraint.

Having heard what was thus commanded by the Queen, they were all awakened; devoted to the practice of the True Dharma, they gathered together and set out. Then that Great Queen desired to see the garden.
Approaching his master, he reported that matter to him.
Having heard what was reported, the king, that lord of men, then had the entire city cleared and decorated on all sides.
Having thoroughly cleansed and beautifully adorned that garden as well as its lakes,
he then placed his beloved wife together with her retinue upon a chariot and sent them joyfully toward the garden at a slow pace.
Having approached that place and beholding that delightful garden, she quickly descended from her chariot and moved about there with joy,
gazing upon that garden adorned with flowers of every season.
It was as beautiful as the Nandana grove, endowed with all fruits;
and its lakes were filled with auspicious waters possessing the eight qualities, as well as with excellent flowers such as lotuses and water-lilies, and with birds. (77–78)
Her heart gladdened by great joy, enthusiasm, and exultation, she wandered everywhere; even as she beheld all things, she moved about with delight.
Having gazed there for a very long time, she wandered about according to her will.
Taking refuge in the shade of a tree, she stayed on the bank of the lake. Remaining there, beholding that grove adorned with flowers of every season and the lake as well, she experienced great bliss.
Then that Great Being, having seen and touched all the sick, desired to restore them to health; she herself approached,
and having informed the king, she received his permission.
Having looked upon all and touched them, she restored the sick to health.
Then, possessing great supernormal powers, she desired to make all the wretched and the poor prosperous by giving them whatever wealth they wished for.
Having reported that matter before the king and received his permission,
she nevertheless bestowed their desires upon all those who were poor and made them wealthy. Then, that woman of great heroism [dealt with] those who were indolent and of cowardly disposition.
Having comforted them, the two women wished to employ them all in their service.
Having informed the king of this and received his permission, they were filled with joy;
and having consoled all those who were distressed, the two of them set them to work.
Then Subhadrāṃśā, having fed all those eminent śramaṇas, desired to clothe them with new garments;
and she reported this to the king regarding all those eminent śramaṇas.
Having fed them, she joyfully clothed them all in new garments.
Thus that queen, the goddess endowed with the power of a great being, fulfilled everything according to her desire for the sake of Dharma. 89–90.
Thus, having conceived that pregnancy-longing (*dohada*), she joyfully performed all desired meritorious deeds such as giving, practicing them with delight;
at that time, auspicious enthusiasm prevailed everywhere in that beautiful realm.
There prevailed a time of abundance, free from calamities and free from disease. At that time, not even a single person there was poor,
nor one devoted to evil, nor one who was wretched, needy, miserly, greedy, envious, or intoxicated with pride.

All became wealthy, of virtuous conduct, generous, seekers of excellent qualities, diligent in the practice of the true Dharma, and celibate. Thus, that queen was pregnant with a noble embryo, a Bodhisattva.
Devoted to the practice of the True Dharma, she observed the bodhisattva vow.
Then, at the proper time, she gave birth to a boy who was handsome,
divinely beautiful, lovely, and endowed with all the marks of physical perfection.
Nourished, gracious, gentle, and captivating to all the world, his uṣṇīṣa-maṇḍala was manifested by great jewels set within it;
from that jewel, divine rays issued forth and spread out. 97.
There, having illuminated everything everywhere, they made even the night like day.
98 Beholding that radiance, all the citizens, filled with wonder, said: "Whose beautiful splendor is this light? 99
Having heard that he had been born, Janaka was filled with joy;
he bestowed gifts as desired upon the ascetics, brahmins, and others. There, Janaka was eager to see his son.
Together with his teachers, friends, and kinsmen, he approached him joyfully. Having arrived there, he beheld his son—
divinely beautiful, lovely, and adorned with auspicious marks.

Having seen the pure uṣṇīṣa, the great jewel, radiant with divine splendor, he was filled with joy; gazing upon it, he stood for a long time in delight. Beholding his preceptor, kinsmen, and good friends, he spoke thus:
"This jewel upon my head is divine and endowed with auspicious qualities; it produces warmth in the cold and radiates heat, yet it blazes coolly in the heat. (104–105)
This is the supreme means for pacifying all diseases and calamities, a universal appeasement that destroys all malevolent actions;
even the water used to wash it would destroy every kind of poison. 106.
And the entire realm would become fine gold upon being touched by it;
and even this flowing water, or whatever iron it might touch, would likewise become fine gold. (107–108)
Thinking thus, he sprinkled all the elements with water that had washed away the dust from those great jewels, and having turned them all entirely into gold,
he gave all that gold to supplicants with great reverence. (109)
"Having made the Three Jewels your object of veneration, always proceed in virtue.
Having heard this command of his, that father, who was like a guru, desired to see whether this might indeed be true. 110–111.
Then Janaka, joyfully taking the water flowing from that jewel, formed a heap of iron and sprinkled it with it;
as soon as that heap of iron was touched by it, it instantly became a heap of gold.
Seeing that, everyone, including the king, was struck with wonder and rejoiced.
Taking that gold, the king, filled with joy,
caused it to be distributed according to their desires among supplicants, such as the Brahmins and others.
Seeing that newborn boy, even all the gods,
their souls thrilled with joy, took to the sky above him and beautified it by raising up divine banners, flags, and the like. 115.
Having struck all the divine musical instruments, they brought forth supreme joy;
they rained down all kinds of divine flowers from every side,
and they also rained down the seven precious jewels upon that abode.

Above that, resting in the sky, the gods, filled with great joy, held a parasol made of divine jewels and graced him with their splendor; thus it was throughout all the worlds immediately upon his birth. 118.
Thus, in all the worlds, as soon as he was born—
Then, free from calamity and filled with auspicious energy, it proceeded everywhere.
At that time, the world was filled with the glory of that Great-Souled One, and even the lords of all the worlds, having seen him, became completely serene. (119–120)
The four world-protectors, the planets, the Vidyādharas with their hosts, and the Mātṛkās also protected him upon seeing him;
so too did all the sages, ascetics, yogins, and practitioners of austerity.
Having recognized him as born, they joined him with auspicious blessings.
(122) The Arhats and Bodhisattvas dwelling in all directions, and even the Perfectly Awakened Ones, seeing him, were filled with serene joy and offered their protection. (123)
Thus, all the worlds— gods, daityas, and humans—
hearing that he had been born and seeing that auspicious festival,
were eager to behold that child, that great being. 124

Thus, even as soon as he was born, that boy illuminated everything, and by manifesting auspicious vigor, he brought great joy to the world. Then, having performed the birth festival according to the prescribed rites, the family priest—
Having summoned his kinsmen, relatives, friends, and companions, he commanded them thus:
"Let this great jewel born upon his crown, which shines so brightly,
become renowned by the name Maṇicūḍa."
Having been called "Ratnacūḍa" by some, that boy became renowned everywhere in the world by that name;
he shone like the moon, beautiful with the auspicious luster of his jewel. 127–128.
Then, protected by eight nurses and joyfully nurtured,
he grew and flourished in due course, shining like a lotus in a lake. Thereafter, endowed with splendor and possessing fully developed faculties and body, he shone forth.
Having been raised, he reached the state of youth and took his pleasure while bearing the welfare of others.
Then, eager for the qualities of knowledge, he resorted to the schoolhouse;
having performed service to his teacher, he learned the scripts in their proper order.
Then that intelligent youth quickly reached the further shore of the scripts; he studied grammar, lexicons, fine poetry, the sciences, and so forth.
Having studied all branches of knowledge in due order, the wise one became fully accomplished.
Having quickly reached the end of all [learning], he conquered his opponents. Then that man of great intelligence, proficient in all the scriptures, also mastered all sixty-four arts and sciences.
Having conquered all those proud ones, he quickly reached the further shore of all those sciences and became the sovereign of all knowledge.
Thus he was the repository of excellent virtues and the locus of the excellence of his character.
Faithful, of noble intention, steadfast, and striving for the welfare of both himself and others; compassionate, a great being, merciful, and affectionate toward the world;
a Bodhisattva of great renunciation, whose body is the Dharma, and who has conquered his senses. 136–137.
Even when giving away his entire possessions, he was resolutely intent;
indifferent even toward his own body, he was exceedingly eager for the virtue of giving, bestowing whatever wealth was desired upon all supplicants with great respect. (138)
Having given away great bliss and joy, he continued his conduct while enjoying [the fruits of his merit].
Hearing of his intense passion for giving, all seekers arrived from every direction with delight and approached to see him. 139–140.
Seeing all of them arrived together, he, with a joyful disposition,
gave them more than they had desired and made them rejoice in contentment.
Then the illustrious prince, who bore the welfare of all sentient beings as his purpose, [proceeded].
He was proclaimed by those in need as "the great king Maṇicūḍa.
Then that Great Being, having caused a vast hall for giving to be constructed, adorned it with beautiful garments and various ornaments.
There, having established all the ritual substances on every side—
water for washing the feet, water for bathing, water for the *argha* offering, pure water, fragrant oil, and aromatic powders (144)—
as well as all types of cloth such as fine cotton, including even garments with fringes;
Fragrant incense and lamps, flowers of all seasons,
as well as foods to be chewed, eaten, licked, and drunk, possessing the six flavors;
likewise, roots, trunks, leaves, stalks, heartwood, blossoms, and bark.

Likewise, various flowers, both aquatic and terrestrial, as well as diverse fruits that are ripe, flavorful, and wholesome, and all kinds of edible items such as sweetmeats and the like. 147. All these various things fit for enjoyment.
All varieties of rice crops and diverse seeds;
excellent medicinal herbs and elixirs endowed with the qualities of taste and wholesomeness; as well as sandals, garments, umbrellas, canopies, and fans. 148–149.
Various seats such as couches with cotton mattresses, all kinds of articles for adornment, and those made of various jewels; likewise, great heaps of all types of minerals. 150.
He established heaps of gold and jewels, as well as chariots, horses, cows, and elephants;
and young maidens of beautiful form, adorned with every ornament,
along with male and female servants, all arranged on every side.
In this way, having established all other objects and every kind of utensil there, he made them all equally beautiful.
Seeing that, the Great Being, the Bodhisattva, [addressed] those who had assembled.
Seeing all those supplicants, he attained great joy.
Then, having honored all those supplicants in due order,
he caused them to be satisfied with whatever objects they desired.
Having made them all content and observing them with great joy,
he addressed them once more with respect and commanded thus: "Sirs, come here whenever you desire for whatever purpose."
Taking each of those from me, may they always proceed toward what is auspicious;
having desisted from the ten evils and fixed their intent upon perfect enlightenment, may they proceed for the welfare of the world after having paid homage to the Three Jewels.

Thus that lord of kings, awakening all the worlds, bestowed wealth according to their desires and established them in the Dharma. Then all those who were seekers, being gratified by what he had given, were pleased.
Taking wealth and enjoying it, they always conducted themselves in auspicious ways. Thus all those people, longing for the virtues of the True Dharma,
performed worship of the Three Jewels and practiced with great enthusiasm.
Then, everywhere for all people who were practicing the conduct of auspiciousness,
a state free from calamity and filled with virtuous enthusiasm prevailed on all sides.
Seeing that, the Great Being, the Bodhisattva, the friend of the world—
Having enjoyed great bliss and happiness, he proceeded to work for the welfare of the world. Then that Great Being, intensely longing for the act of giving,
desired to give away even his entire body, kingdom, and all his possessions.
He had a lordly elephant named Bhadragiri, of massive form and great strength, capable of traveling a hundred yojanas in a single day;
he also possessed a glorious king of horses, a noble thoroughbred of great speed.
Even those two great beings, who could travel a hundred yojanas in a single day, that Bodhisattva— possessing the nature of supreme generosity— desiring to give them away as well,
went about the city looking for brahmins who might seek them.
Having perceived that King Brahmadatta’s mind was intensely attached to giving that [gift], his domestic priest announced it in the presence of his father:
"O King, you should know that Maṇicūḍa has been supported by those who seek his favor. (168)
He even desires to bestow those two who are the very embodiments of Victory and Glory;
yet, even when they have been given by him, Victory and Glory shall not dwell anywhere in his kingdom.
For he alone in whose kingdom these two have gone is truly possessed of victory and glory.
Thinking thus, O Great King, if you desire the glory of victory,
awaken that Great Being and dissuade him from giving himself away.
(171) If that High-Souled One is not restrained by you with diligent effort, [the world will perish].
"Surely he will give even these two lords of elephants and horses to the petitioner;
for then, O Great King, the Goddess of Victory would surely not dwell here, and in the absence of the Goddess of Victory, a great calamity would certainly occur. (172–173)
"Or how else could this be? Indeed, I do not believe this; reflect upon it, O Great King, for you alone are the authority.
Thus was it reported by that minister, the priest Śāsin.
Upon hearing this, King Brahmadatta, his father, became despondent.
Then King Janaka, having suddenly summoned his son Maṇicūḍa, commanded him thus in the presence of the assembly.
Listen, dear child Kumāra, for your own benefit I shall speak to you:
that which you give to supplicants according to their desire is for your own welfare.
Those two auspiciously formed beings, the lordly elephant and horse, are portions of the very essence of the goddess Jayaśrī.
Do you also intend to bestow even those two upon suppliants?
(178) If you give even these two auspicious portions to suppliants, then Jayaśrī will not remain in your kingdom; she will surely depart. (179)
He in whose hands these two auspicious portions— the lordly elephant and the lordly horse— have come,
he alone shall become the king of kings, the sovereign of all the world. At that time, you shall be cast down from your kingdom and abandoned by the glory of victory.
How could you wander like an ascetic in a desolate, uninhabited forest?
(181) Having given wealth to all seekers according to their desires and wishes, how could you, fallen from the dharma of your lineage, live like a beggar in the woods? (182)
Having reflected thus, I have declared this for your benefit; having heard it, O son, do not set your mind upon excessive giving.
For by excessive giving Bali was bound, and Rāvaṇa likewise by his extreme pride.
"Sītā was abducted because of her excessive beauty; one should avoid extreme states everywhere.
(184) Having understood this, my child, you should give what ought to be given as desired, but do not give anything that should not be given to anyone, anywhere. (185)
Even though you are being addressed by me in this way, if you do not heed my words and desire to give away even that jewel which ought not to be given, then,
having abandoned the life of a householder, you shall dwell in the forest like an ascetic.
Give whatever wealth is desired to those who ask and practice austerity.
Even if you should become abandoned by victory and glory and fall from your kingdom,
then your kingdom will be seized and enjoyed by your enemies.
Then, having surely overcome you and bound you in anger, or having placed you in confinement, the enemies will kill you with great effort;
then they will bind all of us as well, or even place us in prison.
Having established [the enemy], their foes will slay them with wrath, treating them with contempt;
then all those seekers of wealth, even those friends who desire their welfare, seeing this, will act with utter hopelessness. What indeed can they do? (190–191)
Likewise, having destroyed all of us, your kinsmen, you yourself will be slain;
having cast everyone into hell, you shall fall and wander in delusion. At that time, what will become of us who desired only the words of your false blessings? (192)
"We would wander about there experiencing nothing but sufferings.
Having heard what I said for your benefit, my child, you should give away the objects to be given and, enjoying happiness, conduct yourself in auspiciousness. 193–194.
Having brought about the welfare of the entire world and maintained the auspicious interests of both yourself and others,
dwell happily in the stage of kingship while practicing the traditional laws and customs of your lineage;
otherwise, you will inevitably experience sufferings.
"Living in that forest, meditate and conduct yourself happily like an ascetic.
Having heard what his father said, Maṇicūḍa was delighted;
having replied, "So be it," he prepared to go to the forest.
Then, having bowed at the feet of his father and his mother and standing before them,
he reported these events and requested their permission. Having heard that, his mother embraced her dear son.
Scorched by the fire of the pain of affection, she lamented and spoke thus:
"Alas, my son! Having abandoned me, where will you wander alone in the forest?
Even if you have great suffering, you should endure it with me for a moment."
Furthermore, since you are my only son and there is no other, who indeed here could bear the kingdom? Having abandoned it, how could you wander in the forest?
Moreover, you are but a youth, and your body is exceedingly delicate.

How could you endure the sufferings of cold, wind, heat, and so forth? (202) How could you dwell alone and unattached in the solitude of the forest—a place frequented by many creatures and a refuge for thieves and evildoers? (203)
Having heard these words of mine and considering the great suffering in the forest,
do not go, abandoning the hermitage of kingship for the lonely and inaccessible wilderness;
instead, give away all objects to be given here to every petitioner according to their desire.
"Enjoying happiness according to your desire, abide steadfastly in the Dharma.
Having heard these words spoken by his mother, her son Maṇicūḍa remained dejected and unenlightened, dwelling in a chamber of sorrow.
And there, the ministers, counselors, officials, friends, and people, perceiving that he wished to wander in the forest, sought to restrain him;
though they all tried with great effort to terrify and awaken him to reason. (207)

Being restrained in the forest, he stood there with his mind fixed on that [goal], like a yogi. Seeing him standing thus, they thought, "Surely he will go into the forest," and becoming despondent, they all soon departed from there.
Then, seeing the people fast asleep at night and overcome by slumber,
he himself rose up and quickly departed from the house;
there, in that city, he beheld [the scene] as he suddenly emerged from the town.
Having set out for the forest wilderness, he wandered alone and fearless. There, seeing him arrive suddenly, a forest deity, having followed him and protected him, brought him to Gautama’s hermitage.
Having approached that place and beheld the beautiful forest of asceticism, he took refuge at the foot of an aśvattha tree and remained there, absorbed in meditation.
Seeing him seated there in that manner, the sage Gautama [approached].
Approaching him suddenly, he beheld that great being Virocana, Maṇicūḍa; thinking him to be such, the sage quickly approached, offered his blessing, and asked the reason for his arrival.
"For what purpose, my friend, do you now travel abroad at night? Tell me that in my presence, if I am dear to you as a friend.
Having heard what was said by him, the prince Maṇicūḍa—
Bowing down to that Gautama and looking at him, he spoke thus:
"Listen well, my friend, to the purpose for which I have come here; I shall declare it before you, for you are a dear friend to me. (217-218)
All these worlds are devoted to the enjoyment of desires and afflictions;
having performed meritorious and sinful deeds, they go to heaven or to hell.
Having enjoyed various pleasures in heaven, they remain deluded by desire.
And by means of their merits, they do not perish, though they are facing hell.
Having experienced intense suffering in hell and being filled with remorse, they turn toward the Dharma and go once more to a happy rebirth. (220–221)
"Thus, having understood the manifold suffering within existence, the wise yogi abandons the life of a householder like poison and goes to the forest of asceticism.
(222) Having thus reflected in my mind, I became free from desire for the enjoyments of saṃsāra.
"Having undertaken the vow of a penance grove, I have come here with joy to take my pleasure.
Having heard what was thus declared by him, that twice-born Gautama, desiring to ascertain his true intention, spoke while manifesting fear.
"O Prince, how can you wish to dwell here in this great forest, crowded with various dangers from Rākṣasas and other beings,
when you have renounced the world even while in your youth, without regard for your own life? (225)
O Lord, you have indeed followed this course of fickleness;
for when this Dharma is practiced by those possessed of right conduct, it is honored whether one dwells in a home or in a forest.
Having abandoned even magnificent palaces,
why do you set your mind upon this forest, subsisting on alms obtained through the favor of others? 227
Treated like a villain by the people, bearing the burden of a cripple, and deprived of kinsmen and friends,
how indeed would you dwell upon the ground at the edge of the forest? 228
How is it that you have fallen under the power of grief, as if embracing poverty incarnate? For,
beholding this condition of yours—
Even your enemies would have their eyes clouded with tears;
therefore, O Lord, go and always protect the kingdom, which is favorable to your own kin, yet now distressed and afflicted.
Dwelling in your own home, you should accomplish both the Dharma and the desires of the people;
for even one who performs labor for others finds his home a source of comfort through its own wells.
"How much more so those who have attained happiness, whose splendor blazes with prosperity! (231) Having heard this, the Bodhisattva remained undisturbed;
having become detached from the enjoyment of sensual pleasures, he looked at him and spoke thus: (232)
Because these words arise from affection for you, they may seem like a small transgression to your desire;
however, never entertain the notion that the domestic life is pleasant. Whether one possesses wealth or is destitute, the state of householdership is a great source of unease.
Since there is no happiness whatsoever for one who possesses wealth— due to the exhaustion of guarding it— and none for one who is destitute— due to the toil of acquiring it—
in such a state, the delusion of attachment is merely the arising of the fruit of evil.

Even for a king, there is no satisfaction in that which consists of the inevitable suffering of acquiring and protecting [wealth], and which is the sole target of calamities such as execution and imprisonment.
Like showers of water from the ocean of worldly existence,
if this calculated suffering does not come upon us, how, where, or when could there be happiness here?
Even when engaging with sense objects, there is generally a conceit of pleasure born of delusion, like scratching an itch; yet one often falls into intoxication through prosperity within the home.
Pride through lineage, intoxication through wealth, arrogance through power, anger through suffering, and despondency through misfortune—
when could there ever be an opportunity for tranquility in such a person? 238

Who indeed would resort to that destruction which is the lair for the serpents of pride, conceit, and delusion, and which is the dissolution of the blissful happiness of tranquility, like entering the mouth of a serpent?

How could the mind find such delight even in the third heaven as it finds in a forest— a dwelling free from the abode of intense suffering— which offers the bliss of solitude found in the home of a contented person? (239–240)
Therefore, even though my livelihood is earned through the favor of others, I take delight here at the edge of the forest, clothed in rags;
yet I do not desire a happiness mixed with unrighteousness.
"Like food mixed with poison, [so is this] for one who possesses self-mastery.
Having heard what was thus spoken, Gautama was fully awakened;
beholding that Great Being, he spoke to him in worshipful praise.
"Excellent, excellent, O Great Being! You alone are wise and possessed of right understanding;
you are capable of remaining here. Dwell here, devoted to meditation.
When he had thus instructed him, Maṇicūḍa was gratified.
Delighting in the meditation of yoga, he whose mind was set on awakening moved about there; compassionate and free from attachment, he was always purified by wisdom and tranquility. 244.
Through his tranquility consisting of loving-kindness, he seemed to rebuke the entire world of men, who were attached to desires, for their engagement in evil deeds.
With minds free from agitation and devoid of any intent to harm one another,
the deer roamed there like ascetics. 246
Through purity of conduct, the restraint of the senses,
the practice of contentment, and the quality of compassion, one wins the favor even of people in the world with whom one is unacquainted.
He became as dear to him in the world as if he were his own son;
through his state of few desires, he was incapable of hypocrisy and had abandoned longing for gain, fame, and pleasure.
He made even the minds of the deities inclined toward serenity and devotion;
then, seeing him as a renunciant dwelling in the forest, [the sages were moved].
With their minds bound by his virtues, they perceived him as their teacher and approached him for the sake of hearing the Dharma, as if attaining the very perfection of discipleship. 249
In purity of ethical discipline, in the cultivation of the faculties, in the non-forgetfulness of mindfulness, in solitude,
and indeed in the mental concentration of loving-kindness and so forth.
According to his strength, he instructed his disciples:
"Listen, sirs, to the Dharma spoken by me in brief; it must be preserved by you."
For Dharma is indeed the supreme protection in times of calamity;
it follows one who possesses pure intention and is rooted in loving-kindness—though its association must end in separation. 251
Bodies end in frailty and deformity; life is as flickering and unstable as a flash of lightning;
therefore, one must firmly practice heedfulness. 252
Therefore, strive to increase your merits through generosity and the ornament of ethical conduct,
for one is turning back toward the difficult terrain of birth.
The merits of the world are the supreme foundation;
for the moon shines with its quality of luster, surpassing the splendor of the hosts of stars.
Having traversed the luminaries, he who blazes with a thousand rays is that very one whose elevation is due to meritorious qualities;
so too are kings and ministers of haughty nature. 254.
By the power of the merit of the lords of the earth, those whose pride has been destroyed by the service of excellent horses carry the yoke of their commands as if they were pleased. 255
Misfortune follows those devoid of merit even as they strive upon the path of policy;
for she is being driven away by those who possess greater merit.
Having turned away from that path of demerit— which is rooted in suffering, bound to infamy, and which, as it were, assails its opposites out of sheer indignation— [he] desists from it.
"Apply your minds to these glorious occasions of merit, which are the means for the arising of happiness! (257) Having heard this instruction of his, they all, with joy, [acted accordingly].
Having replied, "So be it," they were delighted and awakened;
then, having circumambulated that one of great wisdom three times and bowed down, they respectfully took their leave and returned to their respective abodes.
That wise Great Being, having purified the three spheres and established mindfulness of the Perfectly Enlightened One, remained absorbed in meditative concentration.
Thus, the glorious one, even there, gave to those in need whatever they desired.
Having undertaken the vow of the conduct of awakening, he practiced for the welfare of the world;
always accompanied by his friend Gautama, he took delight in the forest of asceticism, engaging in conversations concerning the qualities of the true Dharma.
Then the wise seer named Bhavabhūti, possessed of great supernormal knowledge,
took up residence on a plateau of the Himalayas and dwelt there performing austerities.
One day, at that lake called Mānasa, he—
Having risen in the morning, he proceeded to perform his bath, twilight prayers, and worship; at that time,
a divine and beautiful maiden had appeared upon that great lotus, and for some reason, the young girl wept while speaking in indistinct tones.
Hearing that cry, the wise Bhavabhūti looked all around, wondering, "Whose is this sound of weeping?
There, upon a great lotus, he saw her resting upon its thousand petals.
Seeing the maiden, that seer desired to take her;
having gone there in the form of a vulture, beholding that young woman and looking at her, he himself seized her and went suddenly to his own hermitage.
There, having beheld her endowed with the marks of Subhadrā,
he was struck with wonder and his heart became full of faith; he then performed a birth festival for her,
[concluding] that since she had been born from a lotus, she should therefore be named Padmāvatī.
"Let her be known by the world"— thus he gave her a name.
Thereafter, protecting that girl of beautiful limbs as if she were his own daughter, he diligently nourished her with wholesome food and cared for her with great respect.
Thus being nurtured, her limbs fully developed,
she gradually grew day by day like a lotus in a pond.
Then, that maiden Bhadrikā, with her body fully grown, became virtuous.
Having quickly mastered the scripts in due order, she reached the culmination of all branches of knowledge.
Then, having attained the full bloom of youth and being agitated by the passion of love, she went with her female companions to the garden to enjoy herself.
There, that lovely woman, beholding the pollen of flowers and tasting the nectar, took her delight with a heart agitated by passion;
and she saw the intoxicated bees wandering toward the blossoms.
Hearing the warbling of various birds, she became deeply absorbed in delight.
(276) Then, a certain Vidyādharī named Rayanāvatī, moving through the air, paused for a moment in astonishment upon seeing that divinely beautiful woman. (277)
Then, desiring to see that beautiful-limbed Subhadrā,
she descended swiftly from the sky and approached her presence;
there she beheld her, divine in beauty and captivating to the mind.
Her heart was captivated by the quality of his beauty, and she became full of love for him.
Then, having approached her and joyfully inquired after her welfare, he recounted his own circumstances and entered into friendship with her.

Padmāvatī, too, having seen that lovely and beautiful woman and having inquired after her welfare from all sides, entered into a close association with her. Then, those two, bound by affection, joyfully engaged in conversation.
They became intent on each other's welfare through their practice of friendship and affection.
Then, seeing Padmāvatī—young, beautiful of limb, and manifesting the passion of love—her friend Ratnavatī [was moved]. 282–283.
Having taken refuge in the shade of a tree and engaged in delightful conversation,
she gazed upon her virtuous friend Mādhavī and spoke thus:
"I have traveled through all the worlds and have now returned here."
Having observed that this divine beauty was rare in the world of mortals, and having heard what she said, Mādhavī was filled with wonder;
looking at Padmāvatī, she laughed and spoke thus: (285–286)
"O Padmāvatī, we are mortals, sinful and devoid of supernatural powers; therefore, we are unable to travel through the sky in order to see the worlds.
Having spoken thus, Mādhavī looked at that Raṇāvatī.
Seeing Padmāvatī, they were struck with wonder and spoke thus: "O Ratnāvatī, what object so difficult to find have you seen? Tell us that here; awaken us both to the truth. (288–289)
Having heard what was thus spoken by her, that friend Ratnāvatī looked at Padmāvatī and Mādhavī and spoke as follows:
"What indeed is being said regarding his beauty, form, and excellent qualities?"
"Having seen whom my heart was overcome with wonder, I have come here.
Mādhavī said:
"O blessed lady, who is this most handsome man you have seen in the three worlds?"

In this world, is Kāma alone beautiful? Or is the moon, the nectar-rayed one, seen in its full clarity? Since those two possess incomparable forms, who else could be more beautiful than they? 292–293.
Having heard what she said, the beloved Raṇāvatī looked at Mādhavī and spoke again in this way:
"Is this Kāmadeva, who was consumed by the fire of Rudra’s wrath? (294)
"Or perhaps it is the moon; yet why is it that he who is spotless is considered incomparable?
(295) Having heard that, Mādhavī said: "Who else is more beautiful than him? Tell me of that one of incomparable form whom you have seen. (296)
Having heard what was thus related by her, Rayanāvatī looked at Padmāvatī and Mādhavī and spoke as follows:
"Listen with respect, my two friends; the truth indeed is being spoken by me."
That Supreme Person, possessed of incomparable beauty and form,
who was the son of King Brahmadatta in the city of Sāketa and the son of Queen Kāntimatī named Maṇicūḍa— [he is this one]. (298–299)
That prince was of great majesty, possessed of incomparable beauty and form, with a divine and exceedingly pure complexion, adorned with the marks of auspiciousness;
his uṣṇīṣa was endowed with a wish-fulfilling gem, his faculties were pure, and he was a noble refuge. 300.
The sustainer of all desired aims, the bearer of the welfare and benefit of the entire world; pure in conduct, purified in soul, with the three spheres completely purified;
one who exerts himself for the benefit of both self and others, and who dwells in the four divine abodes.

He is one who exerts himself in the practice of the true Dharma, a hero, a conqueror of the wicked, powerful, invincible, wise, steadfast, a vanquisher of the enemies that are the afflictions, and one who has conquered the senses;
he is devoted to the recollection of the Three Jewels and concentrated in meditation free from envy. 303.
He was an expert in all treatises, arts, and sciences, discerning and wise; he knew various methods, possessed true understanding, and had conquered the proponents of consciousness-only;
he was devoted to the qualities of perfect awakening for the sake of establishing the welfare of all sentient beings. (304–305)
The tamer of the difficult-to-tame, the leader, the sovereign of all worlds, the lord, the master of all sciences, the teacher, the wise one, the counselor, the knower of right policy;
he is disciplined, the protector, the knower of self, truthful in speech, modest, and accomplished. (306)
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is most righteous, a preacher of the Dharma.
(307) What is the use of speaking so much? He is the Dharma itself incarnate, endowed with truth, virtue, energy, prosperity, accomplishment, and good fortune. (308)

"O Padmavati, such a man, endowed with glorious virtues, was seen by me—the son of a king; what I have declared is the truth, never a falsehood. You too are likewise endowed with the splendor of excellent qualities."
"You are a jewel among women, the very embodiment of glory; there is no one equal to you anywhere.
That man is also a jewel among men, a great being of vast supernatural power.
If there were a union between you two, the Creator's act of creation would have reached its fulfillment."
"Therefore, having diligently brought that illustrious man under my control, I shall give him to you as a husband; please grant me your consent.
Having heard what she said, Padmāvatī was overcome with bashfulness.
With tears falling and eyes parched, Galadhā spoke thus to Rayaṇāvatī:
"O radiant one, you shameless woman, why do you speak such mocking words?
Where could there exist a man endowed with such excellent qualities? (313-314)
Having thus raised this objection, she related what had been told; and having heard it, Rayanāvatī looked at Padmāvatī and Mādhavī and spoke as follows:
"If you, O Great Queen, desire that best of men..."
"In every way, I shall now bring them here and hand them over to you.
Having heard what she said, Mādhavī was struck with wonder;
looking at Padmāvatī, she spoke thus to Ratnavatī: (316–317)
"O blessed lady, if you are able to bring him yourself,
it would be right for you to bring him and present him to this fortunate woman.
Having heard what she said, that Raṇāvatī—
Having gazed upon Padmāvatī and Mādhavī, she spoke thus:
"Friends, behold him! Just as I have promised, I shall bring that excellent husband here and give him to her."

Having spoken thus, that woman of great supernatural powers ascended the Puṣpaka chariot and, traveling through the path of the sky, proceeded toward Sāketa. Having arrived there, that sky-walker saw [the city] from her celestial vehicle and descended.
Having gone before Kāntimatī, she beheld her and took refuge [with her].
(322) Seeing that Vidyādharī who had arrived from the sky and had taken refuge, Kāntimatī looked upon her and sat down upon her own seat. (323)
Then that queen, the chief consort, seeing Rañjanāvatī and having inquired after her welfare, spoke thus with respect:
"O you who are the repository of the virtues of knowledge, you who move among all beings!"
"Where is there a maiden suitable for my son?"—
having heard her ask this, Raṇāvatī looked at Kāntimatī and spoke thus with respect: 326.

"O Queen, I have seen a beloved woman, divine and exceedingly beautiful, the daughter of the sage Bhavabhūti on the Himavat mountain; she is endowed with auspicious marks, born not from a womb but produced from a lotus, possessing a celestial form. (327)
"Padmāvatī by name is lovely; indeed, she is a worthy match for your son.
Having heard what was thus related by her, Kāntimatī joyfully looked at Raṇāvatī and spoke to her with respect as follows: [328-329]
"O Sage, what kind of beautiful and lovely maiden is that Padmāvatī?
It would be fitting for you to depict her form and show it to me.
When this was said, she drew her form upon a golden plate.

She showed [him] Kāntimatī, who possessed a form identical to that of Padmāvatī. (331) Seeing that lovely image of her, drawn with a form exactly like Padmāvatī’s, Queen Kāntimatī rejoiced, filled with delight. (332)
Then the mother Kāntimatī, remembering her son who had taken refuge in the forest,
stood there with tears streaming down her face, lost in meditation and reflecting on the means to reach him.
Seeing her with eyes parched by falling tears, Raṇāvatī—
He asked Kāntimatī with great respect:
"O Great Goddess, what is your sorrow that you shed these tears? Tell it to me in its entirety, for I shall surely pacify it. (334-335)
Having heard what was thus related by her, Kāntimatī looked at Raṇāvatī, sighed, and spoke as follows:
"Raṇāvatī, this son of mine, the prince, has become disenchanted."
Having gone to the hermitage of Gautama, he practices the vow of an ascetic.
What man, having disciplined that great being and awakened him, might establish him in the life of a householder and cause him to practice the family vow?
Having heard these words of hers, that friend Raṇāvatī comforted Kāntimatī and, looking at her, spoke thus:
"O Great Queen, do not give way to despondency on this account."
I shall make such an effort that he may take up residence in this house;
having painted a likeness of these two according to the rules and performed the marriage rite, I shall establish their kinship here.
Having sent this marriage-thread and having bound it around the necks of both, the joining of the joints must be performed;
thus, when the marriage rite has been completed, [the union occurs] through the influence of destiny.
"May those two become husband and wife; behold these words of mine. Having heard this spoken by her, Kāntimatī consented, saying "So be it," and desired to act accordingly.
Then, having reported this news before his master and having received his command, he arranged for her marriage.
Then, having respectfully summoned the maidservant Kuntalā, he said:
Having respectfully handed that letter to the sage Gautama, she dispatched it;
having gone there at once and approached him with palms joined in reverence, she bowed to that Gautama of great supernormal knowledge and made this announcement: (346–347)

"O Great Sage, you should know that by the king's command, Kāntimatī is performing the marriage ceremony between Padmāvatī and the prince; having delivered this marriage-thread for that wedding, I have been sent here. (348)
"May you take this and give it to the prince.
Having thus informed him, the maidservant placed the marriage thread before the sage Gautama and presented the *śatabhedi* gem. (349–350)
Having seen that sūtra and taken it with reverence, the sage Gautama addressed Prince Maṇicūḍa and spoke these words:
"O Prince, this was sent to you by your mother after she had given it to her."
"Therefore, you should take this and tie it around your neck.
Having said this, Gautama respectfully gave it to Maṇicūḍa and, bestowing auspicious blessings, personally handed over the thread.
Having seen that sūtra, Maṇicūḍa, his mind filled with wonder, thought:
"How was this marriage arranged for me by my parents? (354) Then, having reflected for a very long time, he became indifferent toward the enjoyment of desire.
Beholding Gautama, he sighed and spoke these words:
"O Great Sage, having abandoned my home and come to your hermitage, I shall practice celibacy here with my mind fixed upon perfect enlightenment. (355–356)

So how could I, having abandoned this, return again to the life of a householder and wander, stained by attachment to the pleasures of women? What vow could there be for happiness in a sinful abode, amidst the company of great enemies that are the afflictions? 357.
How could I venture to take delight in a home where happiness is scorched by the fires of various fears, and where the very nature of things is the destruction of envy, pride, and arrogance? 358
Therefore, I do not desire at all to enjoy myself here in this house; rather, I strive to cast off this very body,
and thus I do not wish to accept this thread.
"I desire only to give up my life.

Having heard this declared by him, the sage Gautama, looking at that great being Maṇicūḍa, spoke as follows: 359–360. "I desire only to abandon my life. Having heard this which was proclaimed by him, the sage Gautama, beholding that great-souled Maṇicūḍa, spoke these words.
"O prince, if you do not wish to practice the Dharma at home,
tell me for what purpose you maintain this body.
(361) Having heard what was thus spoken, the high-minded Maṇicūḍa—
Beholding his friend Gautama, he spoke these words:
"Listen well, my friend; I shall tell you the purpose for which I bear this body. Having heard it, let it be understood. (362–363)

Even those who have heard much and are skilled in all branches of knowledge may become attached to the qualities of sensual pleasure in their homes, tormented by the afflictions; consequently, their hearts are scorched by the heat of the fire of the suffering of the afflictions. 364.
Thus, their inner dispositions are set ablaze by the intense heat of the fire of the suffering of the afflictions.
Having abandoned the boundaries of their own family dharma, they conduct themselves with wicked behavior;
consequently, those of impaired nature become intent upon the ten unwholesome actions— fallen from right conduct, greatly corrupt, and revilers of the virtues of the true Dharma.
Even while engaging in terrible sins according to their own will,
they wander through intense misdeeds, tormented by the fires of fierce afflictions;
consequently, those deluded ones become as unfortunate as bhūtas and piśācas.

With their limbs constantly scorched by the fire of suffering, they die and go to hell. Having gone to hell and experienced the fruit of their own misdeeds, they are perpetually consumed by unbearable suffering and wander forever through existence.

Thinking thus, the wise and steadfast virtuous ones abandon this home in saṃsāra— a dwelling place of sin and suffering— and reside in the forest, which is true happiness. Remaining in the forest, having attained meditative absorption, they are free from afflictions and possess stainless faculties.
Those who have fixed their selves in meditative concentration achieve perfect restraint;
likewise, may I too, staying here in the forest with a mind set on enlightenment, dwell forever having enjoyed the true bliss and joy of concentration.
"Having given this body to those who seek it, I shall indeed go to supreme peace; I will not return home again to practice the dharma of my family.
Having heard what he declared thus, Kuntalā then—
Having gone there, he related this entire account before Kāntimatī.
(374) Upon hearing what was told, Kāntimatī became despondent; afflicted by the grief of love for her own son, she fell to the ground in a swoon. (375)
Seeing the queen falling down, Raṇāvatī embraced her, raised her up suddenly, comforted her, and spoke as follows:
"O Queen, maintain your fortitude and remain; do not despair. (376)
"I shall make an effort so that this prince may take refuge in my home. Having spoken thus and looked upon the goddess, Raṇāvatī then departed from there and dwelt in the hermitage of Gautama.
There, having assumed the form of a female ghost, that Rayanāvatī approached Prince Maṇicūḍa and spoke to him thus:
"O Prince, you are a great renunciant who fulfills the desires of all supplicants."
"Grant me that which was promised by you, so that it may be fulfilled.
(380) Having heard this request, Maṇicūḍa was moved to compassion;
looking upon Pretāśinī, whose limbs were loathsome, he spoke thus: (381)
"O Piśācī, whatever you ask, that I shall certainly grant you;
pray as you desire, and let no doubt be entertained.
Having heard this declared by him, that corpse-eater—
Beholding that prince, the Great Being, she spoke thus:
"O Prince, if you have no desire for the enjoyment of the pleasures of saṃsāra, then for what purpose do you give this body? I shall devour it. (383-384)
Having heard this request made by her, Maṇicūḍa gave his consent, saying:
"I shall give you this body; adorn it as you desire.
Having heard what he had said, that Gautama, out of anger—
To that woman, who had the form of a phantom-eating *māyā-preta*, he spoke thus:
"O you wicked one! You are a Rākṣasī of illusory form; how is it that you desire to devour this prince, a lover difficult to find even in the three worlds? (386–387)
"If you do not go far away immediately, I shall strike you!
Having said this, he raised his staff and went toward her in a rage to strike her.
Seeing him with the staff raised, ready to strike her—
Maṇicūḍa went forward, restrained him, and spoke thus:
"O Great Sage, do not be angry; be gracious here for my benefit, since I desire to give my own body for the sake of attaining the jewel of enlightenment."
Therefore, you ought not to create an obstacle for me here in this great act of giving; please be gracious in this matter and rejoice, so that through this I may attain awakening.
For if one were to create an obstacle here, they would fall away from the path of the True Dharma. 391.
"Thinking that one whose self is scorched by the fires of existence and affliction falls into hell as a partaker of suffering (392),
you ought, having rejoiced in this, to act as my companion in accomplishing the true Dharma here (393)."
Having heard this spoken, Gautama was despondent;
his soul tormented by the fire of affection and passion, he stood there bewildered, looking on.
Then that great being Maṇicūḍa became eager.
Having thus addressed that flesh-eating Piśācī, he said:
"O woman, with faith I give this body of mine to you; accepting it, employ it as you wish for the accomplishment of dharma."
"Or even after eating, having composed yourself with a mind fixed on perfect enlightenment,
and having performed deeds for the welfare of the world, always conduct yourself auspiciously. Having spoken thus, that Great-souled One, full of faith, offered up his own body.
With a very serene disposition, he gave [the gift] to that woman who eats corpses;
having joyfully assumed that body given by him, she, with a serene disposition, cast off her form as a corpse-eater and took on the body of a Vidyādharī. (398–399)
Upon seeing her, that great being Maṇicūḍa stood for a very long time, utterly amazed, gazing intently with an unwavering mind.
Then that vidyādharī [beheld] that high-minded Maṇicūḍa.
Beholding his lotus-face, which was exceedingly serene, she spoke this:
"O Prince, having given yourself to me and surrendered it, you ought now to remain for a year and attend upon me."
"First, having heard my words, you must act with faith exactly as I say; accomplish this and conduct yourself accordingly.
Having heard what she said, Maṇicūḍa was thus awakened.
Having thus made his vow, he became the accomplisher of that task.
Then, having disciplined him who was firm in his resolve, Raṇāvatī, upon seeing the great seer Gautama, addressed him and spoke as follows.
"O Great Seer, since this prince is so divinely beautiful, I am eager to give Princess Padmāvatī to him. Therefore, may you also accomplish whatever task is required. 406.
Since I wish to take him to the mountain home of Padmāvatī,
you ought to come there to the hermitage of Bhavabhūti on that Himalaya along with this prince. (407–408)
Having heard what she had said, Gautama was delighted and desired to go to the Himalayas together with her;
then, accompanied by Kumāra-Gautama, she ascended the vehicle.
Moving swiftly through the sky, she arrived at the Himalayas;
having reached that hermitage and descended from her vehicle, she proceeded to the garden to meet Padmāvatī. 410–411.
Then, having placed Padmāvatī— who was devoted to Maṇicūḍa,
whose limbs were scorched by the heat of the fire of desire, who was as if smeared with poison, and utterly deluded—
upon a moonstone with great care; 412.
Having served Mādhavī with excellent hospitality, she took refuge with her. Seeing her, Rañjanāvatī quickly approached;
observing Mādhavī seated there, she questioned her as follows.
"For what reason does Padmāvatī sit here in Mādhavī’s grove? Or is the queen afflicted by illness? Tell me that in my presence.
When she had been asked this by her friend, Mādhavī looked at her.
He spoke thus to his friend, who was accompanied by the two young seers:
"O Ratnavatī, come here; sit down and take refuge with us. Listen as I speak with the queen concerning the matter for which I am seated here."
Ever since you described the beauty and virtues of Maṇicūḍa, the princess's heart has been colored by passion for this prince;
with her limbs scorched by the fire of that passion, she is deluded as if smeared with poison.
"For the pacification of his fever, this [remedy] has been placed by me here upon the stone.
Therefore, having observed it, you ought to devise a means for the pacification of his fever and carry it out in every way. (419–420)
Having heard what was thus related by her, that Raṇāvatī comforted Padmāvatī and Mādhavī, and spoke to them as follows:
"O Queen, maintain your fortitude and remain; cast off this state of despondency."
"Having given you the means to allay your suffering, I shall attend upon you," she said; having thus comforted Padmāvatī along with her husband and addressed Prince Maṇicūḍa, she spoke as follows.
O Prince, fulfill that vow you made, having established it in truth: "I shall do what is for the benefit of all.
For Queen Padmāvatī is distressed and tormented by the fire of passion.
Having heard her say, "Therefore, you ought to treat him for the sake of calming his illness," Maṇicūḍa, out of shame,
did not even desire to look at Padmāvatī’s face.
Then that Vidyādharī, having disciplined Maṇicūḍa— who had remained silent—
by instructing him through many narratives, exhorted him further. Thereupon, Maṇicūḍa, having heard those words, was fully awakened.
Having gone there, he stood gazing at Padmāvatī with a compassionate mind.
Then the wise prince washed his crest-jewel and sprinkled all of Padmāvatī’s limbs with that water.
By that, the heat in her outer body was pacified;
yet, from the sight of him, the fire of passion blazed up even more intensely. Then, her mind scorched by the fire of passion, she fainted away.
Yet, as if smeared with even more potent poison, she did not regain her composure at all.
Seeing this, he washed his crest-jewel once more with water,
gave that water into Padmāvatī’s mouth, and restored her.
Having quickly drunk that water, she regained her mental composure;
thereafter, her mind attained happiness, longing for his virtues.
Then, the hearts of those two became bound together by mutual affection.

In playing, eating, conversing, looking at one another, laughing, and so forth, from that time on, those two moved about together like a married couple, full of confidence, speaking in secret, and bound by shameless passion. (434–435)
Seeing those two thus bound by affection, Raṇāvatī approached Gautama and Mādhavī and said this with joy:
"O Great Sage, whatever task I undertake with effort shall be accomplished."
Just as this couple moves about bound by affection,
so may you, having won over this prince and instructed him, perform the marriage rites and establish him in the life of a householder.
“Mādhavī, having won over Padmāvatī, entertain her so that these two, bound by passion, may continue to live in the life of royalty.
Having heard what she said, Mādhavī gave her assent.

Having propitiated Padmāvatī, he enlightened her regarding the marriage. Being thus enlightened by her, she—her face bowed down, her countenance divided between shame and joy, and her heart struck by passion—stood there with her head cast low. (440–441)
Gautama, having won over the prince and seeking to awaken him, began the marriage rites with Padmāvatī;
seeing that, Prince Maṇicūḍa became disenchanted.
Having no desire for the life-stage of kingship, he went and took refuge in a grove; longing for the practice of the true Dharma and indifferent to the nature of the afflictions,
he composed his mind in the thought of awakening and remained absorbed in meditative concentration.
Knowing that he was dwelling in the garden, established in meditative concentration and dhyāna, Gautama approached him there and awakened him;
though being awakened by him through various means, he remained unawakened. 445.
Having meditated thus, that great-souled one remained with his senses unmoving.
Then Bhavabhūti, seeing him and remembering Padmāvatī,
approached him, weeping, searching for her as he looked about.
Having heard that lamentation, her friend Ratnāvatī suddenly emerged and, looking about there, beheld him;
seeing him, she approached the great sage at once with palms joined in reverence.
Having prostrated with the eight limbs of the body, she gazed upon him and took refuge in him.
Seeing that Raṇāvatī with eyes parched by falling tears, the great seer Bhavabhūti questioned her thus with great respect.
"Padmāvatī is not in the house; where has Rayanāvati gone? I have not seen her for many days; tell me news of her.
Having heard this question from the great sage, that Rayanāvati—
Having beheld Bhavabhūti, he spoke thus with respect:
"O Great Sage, your daughter Padmāvatī is present here;
she is seated upon a moonstone slab together with us."
Having heard what she said, Bhavabhūti was awakened;
he immediately set out to see Padmāvatī there. Seeing him arrive there, Padmāvatī was filled with joy.
Rising suddenly, she bowed at his feet with palms joined in reverence (455).
Then Mādhavī, seeing him, also rose at once; having offered her salutation with palms joined, she joyfully offered him a seat (456).
Gautama, too, having observed that Bhavabhūti had arrived, rose suddenly and, looking at him, approached to offer salutations; meanwhile,
Bhavabhūti beheld Gautama as he drew near.
Having prostrated and inquired after his well-being, [Gautama] asked the reason for his arrival.
Gautama also, having prostrated before him and inquired after his well-being with joy,
reported all these events and informed him.

Having heard that, Bhavabhūti, rejoicing and highly delighted, approved it; seeing the time for his daughter's marriage and beholding Padmāvatī, who was in the bloom of youth with a radiant countenance, he was filled with joy.
And he desired to bestow [the maiden] as a suitable gift upon Maṇicūḍa.
(461) Then, having taken his daughter Padmāvatī with him, her father Bhavabhūti went there joyfully into the presence of Maṇicūḍa. (462)
There, seeing that prince seated after having meditated, Bhavabhūti, with a serene soul, addressed him and spoke thus:
"O Prince, may there always be prosperity; may your desire be accomplished."
"Arise! Listen to my words; I shall instruct you in what is for your benefit.
Having heard this spoken by him, Maṇicūḍa looked at Bhavabhūti, rose up, and with palms joined in reverence, offered his salutation.
Seeing Maṇicūḍa, Bhavabhūti was filled with joy;
having respectfully addressed him, he spoke these words in private:
"O Prince, since you are wise, divinely beautiful, and accomplished..."
Having heard these words of mine, you ought to practice the Dharma:
take this Padmāvatī, who longs for your virtues and is like a lotus-born goddess, and perform your duty toward your family together with her. 467–468.
Having heard what was thus related by him, he remained unawakened;
with his face cast down and his expression lacking serenity, he gave no reply at all.
Once more, Bhavabhūti looked toward Maṇicūḍa.
Addressing him in order to awaken him, he spoke these words with a smile:
"O Prince, you are a Great Being; why then, having abandoned the life of a householder, do you dwell here in the forest hermitage and practice asceticism as one detached from the world?"
Since you, for the sake of the welfare of all, having given to seekers whatever they desired and having undertaken the vow of the practice of giving, have observed the discipline of awakening—
why now, relying on what here, are you indifferent to the phenomena of saṃsāra?
How could you act like a monk, having abandoned the vow of the conduct of awakening?
For they say that among all dharmas, the dharma of kings is supreme,
by which all worlds, being well-protected, are established in the Dharma.
Without a king here, all beings, their intentions agitated by the afflictions like wild and intoxicated elephants, would roam about according to their whims;
they would enjoy themselves as they please, even while causing strife among women. (475)
Having seized one another and fought, they would wander about due to their sin; then those unfortunate and wicked ones, performers of great transgressions,
their souls tormented by the fire of suffering, would go to a miserable rebirth upon death.
Falling into miserable rebirths, their hearts tormented by hunger and thirst,
and overcome by unbearable sensations, they would wander even within the hells;
likewise, dwelling there as hell-beings, they are constantly scorched by the fire of suffering.
"Those of deluded mind, whose memory has failed, will never lead others onto the path of liberation.
Thinking thus, O Kumāra, if you have compassion for sentient beings, then by protecting all beings through that compassion, you ought to sustain them. 479–480.
If you support sentient beings by giving them whatever material goods they desire, then all those sentient beings would always roam about like bulls;
consequently, being endowed with happiness, they would be devoted to their own respective family bulls. 481
Free from afflictions and pure in soul, they have gone to the abode of the gods.
(482) Having understood this, if you possess a mind of compassion toward sentient beings, then you ought to respectfully seek this lotus-born prosperity. (483)
Being deeply attached to her and established in the stage of a king, always perform virtuous deeds such as sacrifices and thereby acquire the true Dharma;
bearing the welfare of all sentient beings in mind, grant whatever is desired to those who seek it. 484.
Having taken up the vow of the conduct of awakening, dwell happily at home.
Practicing thus in the Great Dharma and leading all sentient beings [in it], having brought auspiciousness everywhere, you shall proceed to the abode of the gods.
Having heard this truth spoken by me, marry this lotus-born Ramā and,
having enjoyed her according to your desire, rule over the sovereignty of the kingdom. Then, having produced offspring and having disciplined them in the excellent conduct of statecraft, [rule].
Having established your son on the path to enlightenment, you should practice [the dharma] for him;
then, having disciplined that son and installed him upon the royal throne,
making him the sovereign of all the world, you may thereafter dwell in a forest hermitage.
"Considering this to be the true dharma within saṃsāra, remain in the householder stage of life,
uphold the vow of the conduct of awakening, and practice for awakening if you so desire.
(490) Having heard what was thus spoken, that wise man rejoiced.
He did not even wish to look at Bhavabhūti standing before him;
reflecting, "How can I go back home again with my mind agitated by distress? he remained absorbed in meditation.
Thus, although that Great Being was being awakened by the seer through various methods and illustrations, he did not at all consent;
even though the seer presented him with such demonstrations in two ways and three ways.
Even though he was awake, he did not wish to hear those words at all.
Then Bhavabhūti, seeing that his mind remained unawakened, his own soul consumed by the fire of envy, spoke thus while threatening him: (494–495)
"O evil-minded one, you have not even listened to my words;
having mounted the funeral pyre, I shall burn this daughter of mine along with myself.
Hearing these words spoken by him, Maṇicūḍa was overwhelmed with compassion.
Seeing him thus scorched by the fire of anger, he reflected:
"How could I, having abandoned the life of celibacy and entered the stage of a householder, dwell with a woman, my mind stained by passion? (497-498)
"Alas! I am ruined, I have fallen from the excellent path of the City of the Fully Awakened One;
overcome by afflictions, I shall wander in the company of hosts of wicked paths.
With his soul dejected by such thoughts, that prince was utterly bewildered.
Having somehow summoned his fortitude, he remained absorbed in meditation.
Seeing the prince standing thus, his friend Gautama approached him, looked upon him, and after addressing him, spoke as follows.
"O Prince, you are wise, discerning, and proficient in all branches of knowledge;
therefore, having carefully considered what should be done here and how, tell me.
For if you do not accept this girl, this seer will be provoked to great anger."
"Surely, having mounted the funeral pyre, he will burn her along with himself.
Therefore, you must consider what is to be done here and how it should be done,
lest this great sin of yours truly come to pass now."

Since this rishi, his soul consumed by the fire of anger, will surely ascend the funeral pyre himself in his rage and burn even his own self, you will incur a great sin here for burning a woman and a brahmin. 505. Therefore, there is a great transgression for you in the burning of a woman and a brahmin.
There shall arise a terrible and horrific [retribution], most cruel among all evils.
One whose self is smeared with this sin, scorched by the fire of great suffering, and overwhelmed by unbearable agony, will certainly fall into hell. (506–507)
Then, in that place, there will be no protector, no instructor, and no friend for you;
all those wicked and extremely cruel beings will strike you from every side. Thus you shall experience sufferings even in all the hells.
Wandering about, afflicted by intense and extreme suffering, one would roam thus constantly until the end of existence.
(509) Having understood this, O great wise one, reflect with a concentrated mind;
this which has been declared by me is the truth—do not consider it otherwise. (510)
If you desire the true Dharma, which bestows benefit upon both yourself and others,
then having heard my words, accept this woman who is like Rati; having married her, take up residence in the station of kingship together with her.
Having brought about the welfare of all sentient beings, always proceed in goodness.
Having acted thus according to your desire, having given to those who seek, and remaining composed, uphold the vow of the conduct of awakening and proceed for the benefit of the world.
Thus, may you always have auspiciousness everywhere and certainly, so that having enjoyed the happiness you desire, you may go to the abode of the gods;
and even in heaven, having always enjoyed happiness, with a mind set on perfect enlightenment.
Having accomplished the welfare of yourself and others, you should always conduct yourself in what is auspicious.
Then, you shall never at any time go to any hell; having always proceeded toward a good rebirth, you should practice only in the true Dharma.
"Having understood this, O knower, and having thoroughly examined it through reflection,
proceed with a concentrated mind wherever you desire.
Having heard this instruction from Sumitra, he—
Having reflected thus, the Great Being Maṇicūḍa thought:
"What has been spoken by this wise friend is indeed the truth;
having heard his words, I shall perform the practice of the True Dharma. (518–519)
Having thus resolved, the wise Maṇicūḍa, being enlightened,
expressed his full approval by saying "So be it," and looked toward Gautama. Recognizing his gesture, Gautama was deeply gratified.
Having addressed Bhavabhūti and looking at him, he spoke thus:
"O great sage, be gracious in this matter; do not harbor resentment in your heart, for this man, having been awakened, desires to practice the duty of a king."

Having heard this command from him— "Entrust this goddess Padmaja to him with faith; having performed the marriage according to the prescribed rites, bring about the union of these two"— Bhavabhūti [acted].
Having replied, "So be it," he whose intention was perfectly serene proceeded;
then that seer, taking Padmāvatī with him, joyfully approached the presence of the prince.
