There, having brought that great being, the prince, who was as beautiful as a celestial being, he showed him his own daughter and spoke thus:
"O Prince, [accept] this Padmāvatī, of auspicious limbs, who was born from a lotus."
"I give her to you as a wife; you ought to consider this well.
(527) Initiated with her, you should always perform sacrifices.
You ought to give me that merit which has arisen from this. (528)
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, the prince Maṇicūḍa,
beholding that great-souled ṛṣi, spoke to him as follows:
"O Great Sage, the mental continuum of another is never transferred anywhere."
"Whether it be merit or demerit, it is experienced by the very person who performed it.
[The other replied: "If this is indeed your pleasure, then let that merit which has been earned by me remain here; I shall perform sacrifices on your behalf while remaining right here. 530–531.

"Indeed, I shall give all this merit arising from it to you," having said this and looked at her, the seer Bhavabhūti, with a serene soul, desired to bestow it upon her. 532. Thus offering it, he—whose mind was purified—bestowed it.
Having bestowed Padmāvatī upon the prince, he departed for his hermitage.
(533) Then that illustrious Kumāra, having married Padmāvatī according to the prescribed rites, took her with him and returned to his own hermitage. (534)
Having enjoyed happiness with Padmāvatī according to his desire, he took delight there, full of joy, for some time.
King Brahmadatta, having heard this account—
He desired to bring his joyful son, that prince, back to the city. Then King Janaka, together with his ministers, countrymen, and citizens, proceeded with great enthusiasm to Gautama’s hermitage.
Beholding him approaching, Gautama, together with his son, suddenly went out from there to meet him, bowing low. There, seeing his father, the prince’s face was cast down in shame.
Having prostrated at his father’s lotus feet, he attended to him from behind.
Gautama, too, beholding him, joyfully bestowed auspicious blessings upon him,
led him to his own hermitage, and seated him upon a pure seat.
Having bowed down to that Gautama, King Brahmadatta, together with his ministers, people, and citizens, took his seat upon that throne; there,
Padmāvatī also [sat] at the lotus-feet of her father-in-law.
With her face bowed, she departed suddenly for her own abode after having paid her respects.
Then Gautama reported the entire account in detail before King Brahmadatta.
Having heard that, the father-king, his heart filled with joy and wonder,
looked at his own son and Gautama and spoke thus:
"O Great Sage, by your effort, may this son of mine become a king."

"Your great task has been accomplished; it shall now reach its successful conclusion. Therefore, be gracious in this matter; I entreat you, so please grant me your favor and make my efforts fruitful."
Since this is my only son, I wish to take him there to the stage of life of kingship; that is my desire. And furthermore, when my father Bhavabhūti gave me to you— 547 —[then...]
Then you, accepting [the truth], spoke these very words:
"Indeed, I could not sustain my life for even a moment without you;
how then, O Lord, has your word now become otherwise? (548–549)
Or rather, O Great King, since you are a Kṣatriya and a lord of men,
how is it that you remain standing by even while watching your wife being carried off by a rogue?
Therefore arise, O great hero, if you have any compassion, O Bull among men!
"By all means, save me; you ought to take heed of this!
(551) Having heard this prayer uttered by her while she was still weeping, Maṇicūḍa rose up and looked toward that Kirāta. (552)
Approaching him suddenly with great respect, he looked at him, addressed him, and spoke to awaken his consciousness:
"Enough, enough! Do not carry off this woman; let her go!"
For she is the attendant of Mārīci, the king of sages;
go quickly and leave this virtuous woman before that great seer of vast supernatural knowledge and fierce asceticism realizes what has happened.
Lest that one of great supernatural power, having learned of this assault by you,
should surely burn you with the fire of his curse and cast you into hell—
therefore go at once and release this virtuous, ascetic woman.
"If, having heard these words of mine, you release her and act for your own welfare," (557) having heard what was thus spoken, that hunter, fearing a curse,
released Queen Padmāvatī and then vanished from that place. (558)
O Goddess, that Dharma went swiftly to the assembly of the gods and related this entire account in the presence of the Lord of the Devas.
Having heard everything he said, Śakra, the sovereign of the thirty-three gods, [acted accordingly].
Together with all the lords of the world, he was filled with apprehension and amazement.
Then Queen Padmāvatī, having been delivered from the fear of the Kirātas, gazed upon that Great Being for a very long time and approached him.
Having approached there, weeping and prostrating with her whole body at the feet of her husband, she lamented thus, distressed by the pain of affection.
Seizing her as she lay fallen at his feet, the Bodhisattva was overcome with compassion.
Having raised her up and comforted her, awakening her, he spoke thus:
"O blessed lady, for those wandering through the existence of the six realms, separation is inevitable;
for whom is there ever no parting from the company of friends and loved ones?"
The state of suffering consisting of existence, birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, and so forth;
the afflictions, intoxication, pride, the frustration of desires, and hostility—thus, in this way, there are always various kinds of sufferings within existence. 565.
Having seen all these possessions, I shall abandon them here and take refuge [in the Dharma].
Having observed all those who are deluded and tormented by the fire of this suffering,
I shall awaken them through diligent effort and establish them on the path to enlightenment.
"Having made an offering to the Three Jewels and having set your intention upon perfect enlightenment,
now practice the vow here for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings.
Having understood this, you too, with a mind set on enlightenment, should adopt my way of life.
"Having made offerings to the Three Jewels, practice the vow of the conduct of awakening.
Having heard these words of mine, free yourself from longing for the realms of cyclic existence, abandon afflictions, intoxication, and pride, and observe the vows.
Having heard what was thus instructed by him, Māra was despondent;
he strove to cause that Bodhisattva to fall away from his vow.
Then Māra, having arrived there, assumed the form of a young brahmin.
Addressing the Bodhisattva and looking at him, he spoke thus:
"O noble sir, this Padmāvatī of yours, though endowed with beauty and youth, is tormented by the fire of the pain of love; she is a wretched woman undergoing great suffering. (572–573)

Therefore, out of compassion, you ought to liberate this woman, who possesses the form of Śrī and follows the dharma of her own family, from this great suffering. Thus, take this queen Dharmiṇī and go to your own city.
Remaining there in the stage of a king, practice the Dharma together with her;
having given to those who ask according to their desire, having performed great sacrifices,
and having brought about the welfare of all beings, proceed as you please.
"In this way, may there always be well-being for you, free from calamity and certain;
and having attained sovereignty over heaven, you shall obtain divine fortune.
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, that Bodhisattva Sanmati—
Beholding that young man and reflecting thus, he perceived:
"Who is this—god or human? By whom has he been sent to harass me, that he stands before me thus, prattling? (578–579)
Having thus observed with his mind, that Bodhisattva of noble intelligence, recognizing "This is Māra," reflected once more:
"This is Māra who has approached to create an obstacle for my vow."
Having thus resolved, that wise one spoke to Māra as follows:
"O Māra, do you not know the Bodhisattva who acts for the welfare of the world? He is the one in difficult practices whom you wish to delude. (581-582)

"Are you being obstructed? Go away; do not stand before me! Even all the lords of the worlds would not be able to create an obstacle here, let alone you, who are greatly deluded, regarding this resolve of mine."
"Tell me, how could you possibly turn him back alone?
(584) Having heard what was said, Māra, with a troubled mind, thought, "This one is a man of great wisdom," and having spoken thus, he vanished and departed. (585)
Then, perceiving that he had departed, the Bodhisattva Sanmati looked at Padmāvatī and awakened her once more with these words:
"O blessed lady, arise; do not grieve here in my presence."
In this world, even after a very long association, separation is certain.
All accumulations end in depletion; all elevations end in a fall;
unions end in separation, for life indeed ends in death.
Having understood this, O auspicious lady, and having heard my words,
you have maintained your fortitude and approached the great seer Mārīci, holding fast to the vow for enlightenment with the aspiration for the welfare of all sentient beings. 589.
"Having made offerings to the Three Jewels, practice the vow of the conduct of awakening.
Having thus instructed Queen Padmāvatī, Sanmati sent her once more to the hermitage of Mārīci for the sake of awakening.
Then Queen Padmāvatī, falling at the feet of the Bodhisattva with her face drenched in tears, looked up at him and spoke thus:
"Alas, alas, O Lord, Master of the World! Why do you not have compassion for me?"
Alas! Woe is me, cursed am I by ill fortune; where shall I go for refuge?
O Lord, Padmāvatī, your servant, consumed by the fire of separation from you, will surely go to the abode of Yama after fixing her mind on the remembrance of your name.
"O Protector, this is my very last sight of you in every way," having said this, she gazed after him, bowed repeatedly at his feet,
and turning back to look once more, was tormented by the fire of the sorrow of her affection.
After a long time, she finally emerged slowly from that hermitage.
Then, having gone there, Padmāvatī, weeping, suddenly approached the hermitage of the great sage Mārīci once again.
Having approached there, she prostrated at the feet of that well-minded Mārīca and, weeping, took refuge with him.
Seeing her weeping, Mārīca was filled with wonder.
"For what reason did he inquire so respectfully, 'O Rodasī'? Then, after a long time, Padmāvatī stood before that great ṛṣi and,
sighing deeply, reported this entire account to him.
Having heard what was reported to him and having beheld that goddess, Mārīci, his soul filled with compassion, looked upon her and spoke thus:
"O Goddess, go to your own country; you have been granted permission by me."
"Remaining in your own city free from fear, observe the vow of celibacy together with your son.
Having heard this instruction from the sage, Padmāvatī joyfully prostrated herself at the feet of the seer Mārīca with her palms joined in reverence.
Then that sage, having raised Padmāvatī up, swiftly sent her through the air to the city of Sāketa by means of his supernatural power;
having arrived there, Queen Padmāvatī was filled with joy.
Descending from the sky, he sat down there upon the palace terrace.
Seeing Padmāvatī arrive there,
all those ministers and counselors approached with joy and bowed before her.
And the son Padmottara, seeing his mother arrived there, joyfully prostrated at her feet with palms joined in reverence.
There, the mother beheld that son of hers, Padmottara.
Embracing him for a long time with a face bathed in falling tears, he spoke thus:
"Is all well with you everywhere, my son?
Having been permitted by the Rishi, I have come, O child, to dwell together with you."
Having spoken thus, that great queen, after inquiring after the welfare of all those ministers, people, and citizens, dismissed them with words of affection. Then,
being honored by all those joyful people, she departed.
Having enjoyed the happiness of royal sovereignty, she lived virtuously together with her son.
By upholding his instruction, all the people were filled with joy;
devoted to the practice of the true Dharma, they always moved about in goodness.
Then, by the power of that merit, at all times and in every place there,
everything proceeded continuously with auspicious energy and free from calamity;
at that moment, in that place, of King Duḥprasaha—
A great plague broke out everywhere among the people.
At that time, everyone there, afflicted by the great disease and suffering, lay down upon their beds, uttering cries of "Alas! Alas! in lamentation.
Seized by incurable diseases and utterly deluded,
people constantly die day and night, casting away their many lives;
beholding that great portent, [the teaching] was set in motion on all sides.
That King Duḥprasaha, being terrified, thought thus:
"Alas! Such a great portent is occurring right here in my realm; therefore, I shall employ every means for the pacification of this calamity. (617-618)
Having reflected thus, that lord of the earth summoned all the brahmins together with their preceptors— those experts in the pacification of such calamities— and commanded them as follows:
"O brahmins, you who are all here, there is a plague prevailing in this place."

"Let them immediately devise a means to pacify this [calamity]," thus was commanded by the lord of men. Having heard this, those brahmins accordingly performed the rites for the pacification of that portent according to the prescribed rules.
Nevertheless, that great pestilence was by no means entirely pacified;
rather, it continued to spread in every direction,
increasing even more extensively through the performance of planetary worship rites and the ritual services intended to appease malevolent spirits.
And despite all medical treatments, she was never once cured.
Seeing this, the protector of the earth, overcome with great terror and despondency, summoned all his ministers and counselors and spoke to them thus: (623–624)
"Sirs, this great calamity here cannot be quelled by any means;
therefore, tell me what other great remedy I should employ for this," the king commanded. Having heard this, those ministers and people [replied].
Having reached a unanimous agreement, all the foremost kings spoke thus:
"O King, there exists a ritual for pacifying these great portents;
therefore, by means of this procedure, ensure well-being everywhere."
Since that king Maṇicūḍa was a donor, compassionate in mind,
devoted to the welfare of all beings, and a provider of wealth for the requests and favors of all supplicants, therefore this great jewel grew upon the head of that generous monarch.
The gatherer of all auspicious purposes, the pacifier of all portents— 629 if this jewel that brings about welfare is sought after and brought by those in need,
then surely it will quickly quell every calamity with its sprinkling waters. 630
Having heard what was thus spoken, the king, fully awakened,
summoned five Brahmins who were seekers of wealth and commanded them as follows: "Gentlemen, go quickly to the Himalayas and [fetch] a great jewel."
"Having made a formal request to Maṇicūḍa, you must by all means take him away.
Hearing this command from the king, all those brahmins replied,
"So be it," and departed from there in high spirits.
Then those brahmins, having gathered there in the Himalayas and searching everywhere while wandering about, arrived at that hermitage.
At that time, the Bodhisattva was also awakening Padmāvatī.
Having passed through that [place], he then took refuge in another dense thicket.
There, in that secluded forest, that Bodhisattva, having settled himself for the welfare of the world, reflected thus in his mind.
When, having fulfilled the equipment for enlightenment, shall I joyfully give even my own body to beggars for the welfare of the world,
just as my mind has now become melted with extreme compassion? (637)
A desire for excessive giving arises for the welfare of the world;
"Surely, a petitioner for my body has now arrived here"—thinking thus in his mind, he looked all around. (638–639)

There, seeing those five brahmins who had arrived, that Bodhisattva, with a serene mind, immediately approached them. Having approached them there, he honored them with great respect and sought to win their favor.
Having brought them to the hermitage, that high-souled one took his seat upon his own throne.
Seeing them all seated there upon their respective seats, he was filled with joy;
having gratified them with edible fruits, roots, and other offerings, he comforted them.
Then, seeing that all those brahmins had been entertained, the Bodhisattva, with a serene countenance, addressed them and spoke thus:
"From where have you come, sirs, to this wilderness, and how did you arrive?"
"Or for what reason should you deign to tell all this to me?
Having heard what he said, all those brahmins, looking with joy upon the Great Being and addressing him, spoke thus: 645.

"O Lord, you possess great supernormal knowledge; why do you not know the purpose for which we have come? Nevertheless, it shall be told—listen, O Lord, regarding that which currently concerns King Duḥprasaha in his realm."
A great pestilence and a major calamity break out on all sides;
though wise men apply the prescribed rites for its pacification, it is not indeed quelled anywhere by any means whatsoever. 647–648.
Therefore, you, who are an ocean of compassion and who bear the welfare of all sentient beings as your purpose,
ought to grant immediately the means to pacify that calamity;
for you are a great donor, a Bodhisattva, and an ocean of mercy.
"You are renowned everywhere throughout all the worlds as 'The Giver of All' (Sarvaprada).
Having heard this name of yours, we have come here;
therefore, you ought to bring success to our great undertaking."
Having heard this request made by all those brahmins, that Bodhisattva, with a serene mind, spoke thus to those priests:
"O brahmins, all of you, for what purpose have you come here?"
"Therefore, I shall fulfill that with all things,
including my own body. Having heard these virtuous words of mine, all of you, with hearts full of trust, ask for whatever object you desire, even from my own body.
Having heard this command of his, those brahmins, filled with joy upon beholding that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, spoke thus:
"O Great King, we have been sent by King Duḥprasaha."
"We have come here to request the great medicinal herb born from your head.
O Queen, if you have compassion even for subjects who are difficult to subdue,
please quickly gladden us by giving the jewel from your own head."
When sprinkled with these waters of purification, even all the most terrible and great portents shall quickly go to pacification;
likewise, all epidemics and all poisons as well.
Merely by being sprinkled with this jewel-water, [all calamities] shall indeed be swiftly pacified.
Through the ripening of this merit, whatever you desire shall always be accomplished for you everywhere in every state of existence.
"O illustrious one, thinking thus, if you so desire, bestow this jewel for the welfare of the world and make your birth in this cycle of existence fruitful.
Having heard what was said by him, the Bodhisattva was filled with joy.
Desiring the welfare of all sentient beings and being compassionate by nature, he thought thus:
"Aha! I am truly blessed that even here these supplicants, intent on their trustful requests, ask for even my own limbs."
"For this penance grove, which is under my own control while I dwell here, must indeed be given away; for such supplicants are difficult to find.
Indeed, I am [ready] to sacrifice this wretched body for the sake of the welfare of even a single being."
I myself would even cut off and give whatever is desired;
long ago, for the sake of the welfare of the great world, I, with a mind set on perfect enlightenment, would have given even this hair upon my own head, were it but a single jewel.

Moreover, I shall finally make this jewel of life and this fragile body fruitful, heartening, and dedicated to the welfare of sentient beings— having long been afflicted by great calamities— along with the King of the Kurus and his kinsmen.
By the gift of a great jewel, I shall make the people of the Kuru king’s realm, who are afflicted by the agony of intense suffering, find peace of mind;
by the gift of a great medicine, I shall make them free from their fever.
"Out of compassion, for this is indeed difficult to obtain, I shall therefore give this jewel to the twice-born immediately, out of a longing for the jewel of awakening.
Having reflected thus, that Great Being was filled with joy.
Seeing all those brahmins, he comforted them and spoke thus:
"O brahmins, today I shall certainly fulfill the desire of the Kuru king by giving you my crest-jewel."
Today, indeed, I shall make your coming here fruitful;
now I shall extract the essence from this pithless body.
Today, for all sentient beings who are tormented by great fears, [I shall act].
For those beset by great calamities, I shall bring about auspiciousness;
I shall increase my mind’s compassion toward all sentient beings,
and I shall terrify all the wicked hosts of Māra who are deluded.
Today I shall cause the abodes of the Māras to tremble; now I shall spread my great fame as one who renounces everything in every direction.
I proclaim myself by the title of Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
Today I shall certainly go to the further shore of the perfection of giving;
today I shall cross to the other side of the ocean of my true vow;
today I shall bring enlightenment near from every direction.
Having soon attained the supreme enlightenment so difficult to find,
I shall in every way satisfy the entire world with the nectar [of Dharma];
having firmly rescued the world from the terrible ocean of the suffering of saṃsāra, [I shall establish it in peace].

"I shall by all means lead them to the secure city of Nirvāṇa. Today, I shall satisfy the inhabitants of the three worlds who desire liberation, through this exceedingly difficult gift of the jewel. (680–681)
Today, with this abundant jewel so difficult to relinquish, I shall gladden the Kaurava people who are always afflicted by intense suffering;
today, I shall cause to grow the autumnal mind that has reached awakening.
"Causing wonder among the gandharvas, humans, yakṣas, asuras, and gods—
when indeed shall I renounce my own body for the sake of sentient beings?
Now, at this very moment, I shall fulfill that which was previously prayed for by me."

Filled with compassion, today I shall break open my head and give you the great jewel embedded in my crown, endowed with infinite virtues; today, having restrained my own intense sufferings through the grace of my mercy.
For the sake of sentient beings, I shall give up my life along with this jewel.
Today I will seize the essence from this worthless, putrid body,
casting it away like a great treasure out of sheer distress at the suffering of others.
"Today, out of a desire for perfect enlightenment, I shall shake the entire army of Māra along with its banners by the gift of my crest-jewel.
Having said this, that Great Being quickly took up his water-pot.
Seeing those five brahmins, he addressed them and spoke thus:
"Come, O great sages; today, for the welfare of the world, fulfill this long-cherished desire of mine."
For the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, I shall always give to you whatever you desire, even at the cost of my own life.
By means of this gift, I do not seek sovereignty in heaven.

I do not desire divine great enjoyments, nor the glory of a lord of the world; nor the great fortune of Śakra, nor the glory of the lord of Māra; nor the great bliss of Brahmā, nor any others such as these.

Moreover, having attained unsurpassed enlightenment, you will diligently awaken those beings in the abode of existence who are arrogant due to their afflictions; having rescued them with great care from being submerged in the mire of sensual desire— 694— [you will lead them to liberation].
Having established them on the path to enlightenment, I would cause them to practice excellent restraint;
ferrying across all those who have not crossed over, liberating those who are unliberated,
and consoling those who are unconsoled, I would lead them to perfect nirvana.
By this word of truth, may this labor of mine indeed bear fruit;
may the intentions of Duḥprasaha regarding the welfare of all beings be fulfilled, and may the aspirations of all sentient beings be completely realized.
"May my unsurpassed awakening be accomplished for the welfare of the world!
Having spoken thus, that great donor, the Bodhisattva of clear intellect,
poured streams of water into the hands of those brahmins.
Then the entire earth trembled, and the moon and sun shone no more;
meteors fell, the quarters of the sky blazed as if on fire, and all was enveloped in darkness. The celestial drums resounded, and the reservoirs of water were dried up.
The trees were stripped of their flowers and fruits, and the deer were terrified; all the birds and living creatures fled in every direction,
and at that time, all the men were scorched by the fire of suffering and affliction.
And all the yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras dwelling on the Himavat mountain,
tormented by the fire of intense grief,
lamented thus: "Alas, what a tragedy for Maṇicūḍa, who seeks the welfare of all sentient beings!"
"The death of this royal sage, an ocean of many virtues and jewels, has occurred.
Lamenting thus, all those inhabitants of the Himalayas wandered about, constantly recollecting that great-souled one.

And in the sky as well, many hundreds of thousands of gods, headed by Brahmā and Indra, gathered to behold that exceedingly difficult feat of the Bodhisattva. 706. Those [deeds] of his were most difficult to accomplish.
Then all the gods also stood in the sky, filled with wonder.
Beholding all those brahmins seeking the jewel, the Bodhisattva spoke thus respectfully, intending to give them his own jewel.
O great brahmin, since this jewel of mine has entered and taken its place at the root of my palate, having grown from my hair,
I shall therefore cut open my own skull and extract it myself.
"I am unable to bestow it upon you with my own hand;
therefore, sirs, diligently cleave my skull apart, extract the crest-jewel yourself, and take it quickly."
Having spoken thus, that great hero, whose mind was firmly resolved upon perfect enlightenment,
established a heart of loving-kindness, took his stand upon the surface of a stone slab, made a firm vow regarding his posture, and, summoning his fortitude, faced the east.
Having placed the two pieces of fire-drill wood motionless upon his two knees,
and having firmly grasped both his cheeks with his hands like conch-shells as well as his jaws, he spoke thus to those brahmins: 713–714.
"Sirs, let my great endeavor here be carried out without obstacle;
for I am established with firm resolve and indeed unshakable. Therefore, having suddenly split open my skull and head,"
"Having extracted [this] with effort, take hold of it as you wish.
Having spoken thus, that Great Being, whose mind was firmly set on perfect enlightenment,
closed his eyes and remained silent, composed in meditative absorption.
Then all those brahmins, having heard his words with joy,
quickly took up very sharp weapons and approached;
beholding his skull, they prepared to split it open.
They stood as if surrounding him to seize the jewel, like enemies;
seeing those fierce brahmins who, having taken up sharp weapons, stood encircling the Bodhisattva to slay him.
There, a deity dwelling in that hermitage, overcome with compassion, suddenly approached those brahmins and spoke thus:
"Alas, what a tragedy! O brahmins, by whom has this ascetic Bodhisattva been [assailed]?"
They stood surrounding the royal sage Bhadrika, intent on killing him.
"Do not, by force, cause the death of this ascetic Bodhisattva, who possesses great supernormal powers and works for the welfare of all sentient beings!"
Having heard what she said, the Bodhisattva Sanmati addressed that deity and, looking at her, spoke thus:
"O deity, you ought not to restrain me."
"Since even these companions of mine are intent upon giving for the sake of attaining perfect enlightenment, O deity, you must not create an obstacle for me in the accomplishment of enlightenment;
for by destroying this great undertaking here, you would incur much demerit."
"O Goddess, in the past a petitioner came to ask for my body; the gods and their hosts likewise created obstacles to his giving. Then, by those sins, all those gods were rendered heedless."
If they had not created an obstacle for my giving while they were wandering in hell after committing many evils,
I would have attained awakening and become a Victor without delay. (728–729)
Moreover, O deity, on this very spot of earth, thousands of times I have made the sacrifice of my body with faith to those who sought it;
at that time, no one created an obstacle for me in my vow for enlightenment.
"Therefore, I say this to you: you ought not to create an obstacle here.
(731) Having heard what he said, that deity was awakened; recognizing his great spiritual power, she became silent and then departed. (732)
Then, seeing all those brahmins standing before him,
that Bodhisattva of great heroism addressed them and spoke thus:
"O sirs, all you twice-born ones, having cut off my head,"
"Having extracted the great jewel, take it quickly!
(734) Having heard what was thus spoken, those brahmins were filled with joy and began to split open his head with sharp weapons. (735)
Then, although being struck on the head with those sharpened weapons, he set his teeth [against the pain], maintained fortitude in his teeth, and remained steadfast;
even though his head was overwhelmed by extremely intense agony, he remained composed.
Having established a mind of loving-kindness, he remained there in silence.
Then those fierce brahmins, outcastes of cruel intent,
split open his skull with whetted stones and weapons.
As his head was being struck by those sharpened weapons,
streams of blood flowed forth incessantly from all sides;
seeing this, all the deities took their places in the sky.
Their hearts overwhelmed by compassion, they melted away, utterly bewildered.
Then that Bodhisattva, struck by those intense pains, maintained extreme fortitude and reflected thus in his mind: (740–741)

"Aha! Even for one such as I, endowed with fortitude and possessed of such vigor, this very great suffering has now arisen, unbearable as it is; how much more so, then, for the cowards dwelling in hell who are burdened by sin? (742)
"How can those afflicted by various sufferings endure this? How?
Having understood their great suffering, I myself, having crossed over the ocean of existence, strive to ferry sentient beings across as well.

"By this merit from giving, having attained awakening and awakened others, and having lifted the world out of the ocean of existence, may I establish the world in the Bull [of Dharma]. Having thus cried out, that Great Being awakened his mind.
As he established [the boy] who was scorched by the fire of intense suffering, he spoke thus:
"For a long time you have desired this in your heart;
when indeed [shall it be fulfilled] with blood, flesh, fat, bone, and marrow?"
"Observing that 'I shall always act for the benefit of embodied beings here,' you indeed sought supreme enlightenment;
today, that very time has arrived for you."
Do not abandon my body while it remains; fulfill this most difficult-to-attain desire of mine before it is too late. 748
"Moreover, O mind, if you always desire to protect the entire world,
then now, having reflected upon this, exercise fortitude for the welfare of the world.
Having thus steadied his own heart, that great hero—
Again, uttering words directed toward himself, he spoke thus: "Alas, what suffering! Alas, what hardship for those wandering through existence in the six realms of rebirth!
Therefore, for the sake of your welfare, I am willing to bear all these sufferings."
"May not even a single sentient being be a partaker of suffering within the abode of existence; may they all always practice what is auspicious and dwell in happiness.
As soon as that Bodhisattva had spoken these words, those [afflictions] of his...
All unbearable pains suddenly subsided.
And the more those fierce and merciless ones, even though they were Brahmans, struck his head from all sides with sharpened weapons, [the more the pains ceased]. (753–754)
In that manner, he increased his great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) toward those brahmins and toward King Duḥprasaha along with his citizens.
Seeing that exceedingly difficult task, those cruel-minded ones [were struck with wonder].
Then, their hearts moved by compassion, they looked at one another and spoke thus:
"Sirs, just as we previously heard, so now we behold the greatness of this noble soul, who is exultant in giving. (756–757)
That he himself, even from his own body, joyfully cut away and gave to supplicants on all sides the flesh, blood, and skin along with the bones—
thus we hear of his marvelous fame for great renunciation. (758)
"Having said, 'That which has now become a thousandfold more manifest is seen directly,' those Cāṇḍālas began to split open the head of the Bodhisattva in order to extract the crest-jewel."
The Bodhisattva, too, having overcome even that intense, death-ending pain through the power of his great heroism, remained without distraction,
maintaining mindfulness of the Three Jewels with his intention fixed upon perfect enlightenment.
Like a yogi who has conquered his own self, he remained silent and composed;
then those cruel and fierce men, having exerted effort, extracted the jewel from the Bodhisattva’s head and took it away as a sacred object.
Seeing that, the Great Being, disregarding his own life and paying no heed to the intense agony, spoke thus to the Brahmins:
"O Brahmins, as long as I do not release my life-breaths here," ||| 764 ||
Therefore, quickly place this jewel in my hand;
by personally bestowing this jewel upon you,
I shall purify my own mind, which is established in perfect awakening.
Having heard this request made by him, all those brahmins said,
"So be it," and placed that jewel into his right hand. Beholding it in his own hand, the Bodhisattva was filled with joy.
Displaying the jewel to those brahmins, he spoke thus:
"Today my birth has become fruitful; even my exertion is now fruitful.
For Awakening is now close at hand, and my heart's desire is fulfilled. (768–769)
Previously this was offered by me through speech and even through thought; now I give it to you with my own hand, out of faith and joy. Therefore, sirs, having accepted this jewel of great qualities—
Let them, by my word, present it to King Duḥprasaha:
"Since this great jewel has been bestowed by me for the welfare of the world, by that act may there be prosperity everywhere for that monarch. (771–772)
Having spoken thus, that Great Being, whose intention was fixed upon perfect enlightenment,
joyfully presented that jewel to those brahmins himself. Having bestowed the jewel upon those brahmins, he was filled with great delight.
Astonishing the entire world and eager for the welfare of all sentient beings,
he considered his exertion to have borne fruit; having resolved upon supreme enlightenment and having relaxed his application, he remained silent for a moment.

When his practice was brought to a halt, the steadfast Bodhisattva, having fainted, suddenly fell to the ground, his mind no longer composed; then, by the deity dwelling in that hermitage, [the state of] the Great-souled One... 776.
In order to fulfill the Bodhisattva’s aspiration for the true Dharma,
all those twice-born ones were suddenly impelled through the air by their supernatural power and arrived in an instant before King Duḥprasaha.
There, all those brahmins, having presented that jewel to King Duḥprasaha, took their seats before him.
Seeing that jewel, the king’s mind was filled with wonder.
Addressing those brahmins and looking at them, he asked thus:
"O brahmins, how did you extract this jewel from the head of that royal sage? Let it be told how you took possession of it."
Then, having related this account— how he himself had extracted it from his own head and given it— they awakened that king to understanding.
Having heard that, the protector of the earth was filled with a mind agitated by wonder.
Reflecting upon the Bodhisattva’s exceedingly compassionate disposition toward sentient beings, contemplating the great festival of unattached renunciation even of his own body,
and considering his mental forbearance and gentleness even toward enemies.

Having called to mind that illustrious Great Being, the Bodhisattva of great supernatural power, he rejoiced with a serene soul, awakened [from his delusion]. Then, taking that jewel and bowing down, the lord of men—
Having placed [the vessel] in the hand of the preceptor, he washed it with auspicious waters.
With those waters, that king sprinkled everywhere throughout his entire realm, even in every single house, and thus purified it thoroughly.
Then, as soon as that water was sprinkled, that calamity of the king suddenly subsided throughout his entire realm.
Thereafter, for that lord of the earth, throughout his entire realm at that time—
Free from calamity and filled with great energy, it proceeded on all sides. Seeing that, the protector of the earth, together with his ministers, country-folk, and citizens,
attained the happiness of great joy and rejoiced, being deeply gratified.
Then, beholding the Bodhisattva fallen upon the ground, all those gods stationed in the sky were tormented by the fire of intense grief:
"Alas, alas! What a tragedy! This Great-Souled One has been slain by these evil-minded ones."
Thus they wandered about, lamenting with a single voice;
then, observing these great omens of portents on all sides, the seer Mārīci’s heart was filled with wonder.
"What indeed is this portentous sign that has arisen now?"— thus reflecting with a dejected soul, he stood gazing all around.
At that time, there was a deity who dwelt in the hermitage of that great seer.

He related this entire episode in detail. (796) Having heard this report, Mārīci, tormented by grief, went at once with his disciples and through supernatural power to the hermitage of the Bodhisattva. (797)
Seeing that crest-jewel fallen upon the ground, Mārīci approached it, observed it closely, and thought thus:
"This is surely a high-souled Bodhisattva; he must be the Lord of Sages."
"Therefore, he is worthy of honor and worship even by all the lords of the world.
Having reflected thus, that great seer, together with his five hundred disciples,
beholding that Great Being, took up residence there in a secluded spot.
And so, the goddess also related this entire episode in detail before the sage Bhavabhūti;
having heard it, Bhavabhūti’s heart was filled with wonder.
With his supernatural power, he went together with his disciples to the city of Sāketa.
Having descended there, he stood before Padmāvatī and her son and related this entire matter in detail.
Having heard that, the great queen Padmāvatī was overcome with grief, and Prince Padmottara also became scorched by the fire of sorrow.
Then Bhavabhūti [addressed] that Queen Padmāvatī and her son...
Taking with him Prince Padmottara, along with his ministers, citizens, and townspeople, as well as the women of the inner apartments, the counselors, and the elite troops of the army,
he suddenly departed through the air by means of supernatural power and went to the Himalayas.

There, having seen that great being falling to the surface of the earth, Padmottara the prince, along with his mother and the people, suddenly approached and, observing him, retreated to a secluded spot. 807. Padmottara the prince, together with his mother and the people as well, [did the same].
Beholding his father, he immediately approached him;
there, weeping and prostrating at the lotus-feet of that Janaka along with his mother, he stood in a secluded spot, looking on in deep despondency.
Then Śakra, beholding him falling to the earth, his jewels shattered and his body overcome by agony, was impelled by compassion [and thought]:
"May this Great Being, having made the world auspicious, not [perish]! (810)
"Overcome by unbearable pain, he might suddenly give up his life"—
with his mind thus consumed by such anxiety, he arrived in haste and immediately smeared that body with medicinal herbs of instant power.
Then, as soon as it was smeared upon him, his suffering from pain was completely stilled; sighing deeply as if having awakened from a pleasant sleep, he looked around.
Seeing that, all the sky-dwellers, the gods, and even the celestial nymphs [were amazed].
The Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Yakṣas, Siddhas, and Vidyādharas,
as well as the Sādhyas, the Grahas, the Tārās, and others possessed of great supernatural powers,
were filled with joy, thinking, "This Great-Souled One has been restored to life."
Then, all of them, being delighted, rained down all kinds of flowers and all kinds of fragrances from every side; and,
filled with joy, they played all kinds of musical instruments.
And during that great festival, they scattered even celestial garments;
at that very moment, that Great Being, endowed with the power of fortitude and heroism, regained consciousness, rose up, and looked about in every direction.
There, beholding that entire assembly standing before him, that Great Being, his mind overwhelmed with wonder, thought:
"What is this? Is my mind deluded, or is a dream being seen by me?"
Having thus meditated and composed himself, he remained there, diverting his mind.
Then, seeing that the Bodhisattva had regained consciousness, Mārīci approached him and, looking at him, spoke as follows: (820–821)
"O royal sage, what is this extraordinary deed that you have undertaken? You ought to explain it to us all so as to enlighten us.
Having heard what was thus said, that Bodhisattva Sanmati—
Beholding Mārīcī, who possessed great supernormal knowledge, he spoke thus:
"O Great Seer, this is indeed the conduct of those who practice for enlightenment and have correctly entered the initiation for the sake of attaining unsurpassed wisdom."
Having heard this, the high-souled Mārīci, filled with wonder,
looked again at that Great Being and spoke thus:
"O royal sage, [this is not] yours [to do] regarding these evil-minded executioners."

Even if one were to harbor a thought of malice toward those who possess fierce and extremely cruel minds, who are pitiless evildoers, and who are supposedly splitting open skulls with sharp weapons— this [thought] would indeed be real. (826–827)
Having heard what was thus spoken, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati, looking toward Mārīci, spoke again with joy:
"How [can this be] regarding these good friends who are companions in the practice of awakening? (828)
I might corrupt my mind in the presence of those who grant my desired objects;
I might even betray myself or my kinsmen, relatives, and friends,
but I would never do anything displeasing to these spiritual friends (dharmamitra).
Indeed, I forgive even the offenses of those who would kill me;
I do not commit even the slightest offense against sentient beings—those whom, by pleasing, one may attain great supernatural power, and by offending, one becomes a partaker of calamity. (831)

I would always act for their benefit even at the cost of my own life; for by propitiating these very beings here, one may attain complete perfection— therefore, there is no other field of accomplishment for sentient beings even throughout the entire world.
Indeed, all these sentient beings are bestowers of the qualities of the True Dharma;
they are wish-fulfilling jewels, cows of plenty, auspicious jars, wish-granting trees, and fulfillers of the heart's desires for the accomplishment of all aims. 834.
Therefore, I must always propitiate them like a guru and like a deity. For the sake of their welfare and happiness, endowed with great vigor and strength,
I am prepared to remain in the fires of hell for thousands of eons.
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, Mārīci was gratified; looking upon that Bodhisattva, the Mahāsattva, he spoke as follows:
"Excellent, excellent, O Mahāsattva! That your fortitude is so exceedingly great!"
Oh, how firm is your vow, you who seek the welfare of all sentient beings! Oh, how free from attachment is your eagerness to give away even your own body!
Oh, what compassion you have for sentient beings! Oh, what longing you have for generosity! 838–839
That it is well that you, out of such compassion, have now extracted the great jewel of your own hair and bestowed it upon the twice-born;
by this gift, may you obtain whatever you desire.
"Therefore, you ought to instruct me truly on that matter.
Having heard what was thus spoken, the Bodhisattva, being inspired with faith, looked upon that highly wise Mārīci and spoke as follows: 841–842.
O Kāśyapa, having attained supreme enlightenment through this gift,
may I satisfy the world with the great jewels of the glory of the True Dharma;
having rescued them from the ocean of existence, may I awaken them through diligent effort.
Having established them on the path to enlightenment, I would cause them to practice excellent restraint (844).
Having made all those Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas who practice the conduct of Samantabhadra, into sons of the Buddha, I would cause them to act for the welfare of the world (845).
"O Great Sage, it is for this reason that, being intent on the welfare of the three realms,
I perform this act of giving solely out of a desire for perfect enlightenment.
Having heard what was thus declared by him, that one of great intelligence—
Mārīci, beholding that Great Being, spoke thus:
"How is it known, O Fortunate One, that by giving this gift you will attain Great Enlightenment for the welfare of the world? (847-848)
Having heard what was said by him, the Bodhisattva remained silent for a moment, and then, looking at that seer,
spoke thus: "O Great Seer, this jewel which has been given by me is for the welfare of the world."
"I shall now perform this empowerment of the samādhi of truth; listen!
Having said this, he established a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, maintained his vow for perfect awakening, and spoke these verses: 851.
Just as today, having given my own body out of the power of compassion to one who is intent upon awakening,
my mind has not become filled with regret.
And [may my body be] free from stinginess and dejection;
by this truth, by these well-spoken words,
and by the power of my merit, may my body—
"Let this be just as it was in the past, perfectly beautiful in its entirety"— as soon as he had spoken these words, by the power of that Bodhisattva’s truth, [it became so].
Instantly his body became as excellent as it was in the past;
likewise, by the power of the true Dharma, a great jewel appeared upon his head, twice as excellent as before, like a *uṣṇīṣa*.
Seeing that, the entire earth, together with its oceans and mountains, trembled violently as if its heart were filled with wonder and joy;
even the winds blew gently, cool and fragrant with the scent of flowers.
All the directions became serene, and the sun and moon shone brilliantly.
Celestial drums resounded, and a rain of flowers fell from the sky;
everywhere, auspicious enthusiasm proceeded without interruption.
Seeing that wonder, the gods stationed in the sky were filled with joy;
uttering cries of "Hāhā!", they moved through the atmosphere.
Some scattered flowers, while others cast down divine garments.
Some [offered] ornaments resplendent with divine qualities; some played various kinds of divine musical instruments;
and some rained down divine jewels interspersed with flowers.
Then Jambudvīpa shone, covered with divine jewels;
all sentient beings, having attained the bliss of great joy, moved about, as did the gods upon beholding that divine, wonderful, and inconceivable manifestation. 862.
The sages and the world-protectors all likewise spoke with joy:
"O, the majesty of the True Dharma! O, the power of truth!
For such a great marvel as this is not seen anywhere else in truth."
Thus all those immortals, the lords of the worlds, along with the sages and all the worlds, moved about joyfully proclaiming this. Then the sage Mārīci [addressed] the Bodhisattva Sukāyita.

Seeing him, his eyes wide with wonder and his heart filled with joy, he approached with palms joined in reverence; then, encouraging his intention, propitiating him, and addressing him while gazing upon him, he spoke thus: (866–867)

"Excellent, excellent, O Great Seer! Your mind is indeed well-settled, your vow is unshakable, and your compassion for sentient beings is great—since even regarding such teachings that cause terror, you remain thus steadfast in the practice of great generosity. (868)
For a bodhisattva who is confident, undisturbed, and untiring—
by means of such excellent vigor, conquering all Māras and swiftly attaining unsurpassed awakening, may you become a sovereign of the Dharma. (869–870)
Having thus propitiated him, that Mārīci of great supernatural power went suddenly to his own hermitage together with five hundred disciples;
likewise did Bhavabhūti, accompanied by his assembly of disciples.
Having propitiated that Bodhisattva, he departed for his own hermitage filled with joy.
(872) Then all the lords of the worlds, including Brahmā and the king of the gods, having likewise propitiated that Bodhisattva, returned to their respective abodes with delight. (873)
Then King Padmottara, having bowed at the lotus-feet of his father, with his face smeared with tears and his hands joined in reverence, spoke thus along with his attendants:
"Be gracious, O Lord; do not abandon us, who are helpless and afflicted by grief."
Therefore, come; having enjoyed sovereignty once again, [protect] all the subjects as well.
Otherwise, we shall all surely meet our end right here, consumed by the fire of the affliction of grief, left without hope.
Having heard what was thus spoken by his son, the Bodhisattva, overcome with compassion and awakened, agreed,
saying "So be it," and resolved to go to the city.
At that time, those four Pratyekabuddhas arrived.
Addressing that Bodhisattva while gazing upon him, they spoke thus:
"Excellent, excellent, O Great King! This which you have now done is truly splendid, in that, having entered the stage of a king, you desire to protect the worlds."
O King, if you have not resolved to go to the city,
then Prince Padmottara, along with his mother who has lost all hope, and the entire body of people residing in your realm [will depart]. 880.
"Surely, having vomited blood, he would have passed away;
therefore, come with us, go and established in the hermitage of kingship, conduct yourself while protecting all the worlds according to dharma. (881–882)
Having thus instructed him, those Pratyekabuddhas,

possessing great supernatural power, took that Bodhisattva— who had been awakened— along with his wife, his children, and his attendants, and traveled through the sky by means of their miraculous powers.

They suddenly arrived at the beautiful city of Sāketa. Having descended there, those Buddhas established the Bodhisattva along with Nandana and the assembly of women in that city, and then they departed.
Seeing them all gone into the sky, the Bodhisattva, together with his son,
stood gazing at them with palms joined in reverence, his mind fixed entirely upon them. Then all those Sugatas, by means of their supernatural power, [proceeded] through the air.
Illuminating the world, they returned to their own hermitage.
(887) Seeing that Bodhisattva arrive accompanied by the queen, his sons, and the people, all the citizens were filled with joy and bowed down to him. (888)
Seeing them all so joyful, the Bodhisattva was also delighted;
having inquired after the welfare of everyone, he inspired their minds with high resolve.
Then that king, his own son, [addressed] his father, the sovereign of men.
Having been installed upon the royal throne, he remained there and partook [of the kingdom].
There, that Bodhisattva, established in the life-stage of royalty,
acted according to the bodhisattva vow after performing what is beneficial for all sentient beings.
Having heard this account, King Duḥprasaha was overcome with amazement and thought thus within his own mind:
"Oh, the majesty of the true Dharma! Oh, the fortitude of the mind! (892)
Oh, the fortitude of the Bodhisattva who desires perfect enlightenment!
For that Bodhisattva of great supernormal knowledge, bearing the welfare of others,
would surely become a sovereign king upon the surface of the earth.
"Therefore, having placed myself in the protection of that lord of the earth and always performing service, I shall move about protecting the subjects"—
having thus resolved in his mind, that king Duḥprasaha [acted]. 895.
Accompanied by his fourfold army, he proceeded there with haste.
Having approached that place and bowed at the feet of the Bodhisattva, he took refuge in him with palms joined in reverence.
Then, having propitiated that Great Being and pleased him,
with a perfectly serene disposition and beholding him, he addressed him thus: "O Lord,
you are the Master of the World, the bearer of the welfare of all sentient beings."

The Bodhisattva, possessing great supernormal knowledges, the sovereign lord of all phenomena—O Teacher, I take refuge in you; whatever offense I have committed against you, you ought to forgive it in every way. (899–900)
"You alone are the great king, and we are all your followers; therefore, having granted us the favor of your command, it behoves you to protect us.
Having heard this prayer from him, that Bodhisattva—
Beholding that King Duḥprasaha, he spoke thus:
"Friend, you are my noble companion in the accomplishment of the True Dharma; therefore, always remain joyful in this matter and never despair."
If you always desire what is affectionate, beneficial, friendly, and dear to me, then, O auspicious one, conduct yourself with composure,
always refraining from the ten sins and restraining others as well. 904.
"Establish them on the path to enlightenment and practice it yourself while practicing.
(905) Having heard these words of mine, if you always act accordingly, then your abiding in a relationship of affection toward me will certainly be constant. (906)
Having heard what was thus instructed by him, that lord of the Kurus,
being awakened, responded "So be it" and rejoiced.
Then that Bodhisattva [addressed] that king, Duḥprasaha.
Having given the desired object, he sent him back to his own realm.
Then that lord of the Kuru land, having bowed to the Bodhisattva and taken leave of him, departed for his own territory with great enthusiasm and joy.
There, having reached his own city, he proceeded toward what was auspicious, upholding the instruction of the Bodhisattva upon his head while protecting the worlds;
likewise, all the people, maintaining his command, remained composed.
Having desisted from the ten evils and always practiced the true Dharma, then,
by the power of that merit, everywhere and at all times, everything proceeded continuously with auspicious energy and free from calamity.
Thus, having heard of his great fame, other kings also set out in haste to hear the true Dharma of that Bodhisattva;
having arrived there and beheld that sovereign of men, they [approached him].
Joyfully they attended upon the Bodhisattva of great supernormal knowledges.
There, all of them bowed at the feet of that Bodhisattva and, making this request with reverence, went for refuge.
Victory to you, O God, Great King! We have taken refuge in you; therefore, it behoves you to grant us your command so that we may all carry it out.
Whatever has been commanded by you, in that manner shall we act.
"O Lord, you ought to make this our prayer bear fruit.
(917) Having heard what they requested and having reflected upon it, the Bodhisattva looked at all those kings and, addressing them, commanded thus: (918)
"Sirs, if you have truly taken refuge in me, then you ought to always act by upholding my instruction. Having heard this command of his, all those kings—
Beholding that Bodhisattva and gazing upon him, they spoke thus:
"It is indeed true, O Great King, that having taken refuge in you and having borne your command upon our heads, we shall certainly proceed."
Having heard what was thus spoken, the Bodhisattva, being fully awakened,
looked upon all those kings and, addressing them, spoke as follows:
"If these words of yours are true, then desist from the tenfold evil."
Having undertaken the vow of the conduct of awakening, proceed with concentrated minds.
Likewise, having diligently awakened all the worlds and established them on the path to awakening, always cause them to practice what is virtuous.
"Having thus upheld my teaching, if you wish to practice, take wealth from me and give gifts as you desire;
enjoy pleasures according to your wish, and always act for the benefit of sentient beings. (925)
Having made the Three Jewels your vessel, proceed with concentrated minds.
If you do so, there will certainly be constant well-being for you everywhere, free from calamity and full of great energy; and in the end, your destination will be a happy rebirth.
"If it were not so, there would always be great calamities and turmoil here, various sufferings, and ultimately rebirth in the miserable states.
Thinking thus and composing oneself, one should desist from the path of evil. 928.
"Having taken up the vow of the conduct of awakening, proceed for the welfare of the world.
Having heard this command of his, all those kings replied, "So be it," and being thus enlightened, they rejoiced.
Then that Bodhisattva, perceiving that they were all awakened, made them content by providing them with whatever goods they desired and dismissed them.
Thereupon, all those rulers of the earth were gladdened by the bliss of the true Dharma.
Having addressed the Bodhisattva and bowed to him, they each departed for their own hermitages (932).
Likewise, all those kings, having taken refuge in their respective countries, desisted from evil paths and took recourse in the path to enlightenment (933).
Having honored the Three Jewels and given to those in need whatever they desired and according to their wishes, and having enjoyed happiness while practicing with great enthusiasm,
you thus turned all the worlds away from the path of evil. 934.
Having established them on the path to enlightenment, he always caused them to practice what is virtuous.
Likewise, all those people, having desisted from the path of evil,
venerated the Three Jewels and became practitioners of the four sublime abodes.
Having given whatever wealth was desired to those who sought it, they were filled with joy;
and having enjoyed happiness according to their wishes, they conducted themselves with composure.
At that time, through the power of this merit, there was no calamity and all was most auspicious.
Among those objects of the senses, there was always [detachment] for all those rulers of the earth.
(938) Thus that lord of all lands, the Bodhisattva, the sovereign of men, awakened all the people dwelling in Jambudvīpa. (939)
Having turned them away from the ten evils, having given them wealth as they desired,
and having established them on the path to enlightenment, he protected and guided them;
likewise, all those people held fast to his instruction.
Having desisted from the ten evils and abiding in the four divine abodes (brahmavihāra), they gave whatever wealth was desired to those in need and were filled with joy;
having paid homage to the Three Jewels, they always practiced what is auspicious. (941–942)
Then, through the power of this merit, throughout Jambudvīpa there proceeded incessantly an absence of calamities and an auspicious surge of prosperity.
At that time, however, there was a certain poor man, a seeker of wealth, who was miserly, wicked, and deceitful.
Nowhere on the entire surface of the earth was there a soul tormented by the pride of afflictions (kleśābhimāna).
All beings were free from afflictions, possessed of excellent morality and pure faculties; they became givers of pure nature, practicing for the sake of awakening. 944–945.
Thus that Lord of all worlds, himself walking upon the path to enlightenment,
established and protected all worlds, and moved about with joy;
thus he was endowed with the bliss of the abundant glory of the true Dharma of enlightenment.

Having long worked for the benefit of sentient beings, he remained there practicing what is auspicious. (947) At that time, no man who passed away fell into an evil rebirth; indeed, all of them, having cast off their bodies at the proper time, went to the abode of the gods. (948)

Thus the illustrious one of great supernormal knowledge, having established the world in the practice of Dharma and having caused it to venerate the Triple Gem, remained for a long time in great bliss.
Then, after some time, that Bodhisattva was overtaken by old age.
Having grown old, he became dispassionate toward existence, his intention firmly established in perfect enlightenment.
Then, having installed his steadfast son Padmottara upon the royal throne and made him the king, he appointed him as the sovereign of the entire kingdom.
Then that Bodhisattva, having abandoned that royal hermitage and taken refuge in a forest hermitage, practiced the discipline of yoga.
Having remained thus for a very long time, he lived as a celibate practitioner, composed in meditation.
Having abandoned his body at the proper time, he went to the Brahma-world.
There, having been born with a purified soul, that best among those who know the yoga of Brahma became at that time the Great Brahma— the teacher and sovereign of all dharmas.
Thus, that Blessed One, the Protector, the Teacher Śākyamuni, was formerly the Bodhisattva King Maṇicūḍa, a great donor;
at that time, while practicing the vow of the conduct of awakening, he was that very Great Being. 955.
For the benefit of the world, he bestowed upon all seekers whatever they desired;
having himself cut out his own body, he—whose mind was fixed on perfect enlightenment—gave blood, flesh, bones, marrow, and so forth to those noble seekers according to their wishes. (956–957)
Having given his son, his virtuous and beloved wife, even his jewels, and his very hair as gifts according to their desires, he enlightened all the worlds,
turning them away from the paths of evil and establishing them as dwellers in the Brahma-abodes.
Having established [beings] on the path to enlightenment and always promoting what is virtuous,
having made the world consist of the Dharma and taken refuge in the Three Jewels, and holding the aspiration for perfect awakening, he moved about for the welfare of the world. 959–960.
Through the ripening of this merit, having conquered all the hosts of Māra,
free from afflictions and an Arhat, he attained awakening in the Kali age and became a Sugata. She who was Queen Padmāvatī was the virtuous Yaśodharā.
He who was King Padmottara became Rāhula, the son of the Jina;
he who was the priest named Brahmaratha, the twice-born preceptor,
is now the Arhat monk Śāriputra, the great sage endowed with the great superknowledges.
The sage Bhavabhūti was that Ānanda of great intelligence;
the sage Mārīci was that Kāśyapa, the supreme among disciples;
and he who was the father of King Maṇicūḍa was Brahmadatta. (964)
The great king Śuddhodana was indeed the father of the Perfectly Awakened One; and she who was the mother of Maṇicūḍa, the virtuous Queen Kāntimatī,
was the Great Queen Māyā, the mother of the Blessed One.
Maudgalyāyana, you should consider that he who was the Māra Dūṣī at that time, possessing supernatural powers and assuming the form of a Rākṣasa, and who emerged from the fire-pit as Śakra—
he was then the monk named Nāgira.
Those who were the ministers and the assembly of counselors of that Maṇicūḍa are these five hundred Śākyas, Bhadrika and the others;
and he who was King Duḥprasaha was at that time Devadatta.
The four brahmins who, having extracted the jewel, gave it away were Kātyāyana, Aniruddha, Pūrṇa, and Subhūti;
for in this way the Blessed One performed that most difficult act of giving in the past.
Having taken up the vow of the conduct of awakening, he practiced for the welfare of the world;
likewise, having fulfilled all the perfections in their proper sequence for the sake of the benefit of all sentient beings, he attained perfect enlightenment.
Thinking thus, all those who desire a good rebirth ought to listen with faith and joy to the True Dharma of the Teacher of the World;
those who listen to the True Dharma of the Teacher of the World with faith and joy [attain it]. (973)
They do not go to an evil destiny, but always attain a good destiny for as long as they live.
Born only in good destinies, taking refuge in the glory of the Dharma and excellent virtues, they become Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, who practice the conduct of awakening. 974–975.

"Therefore, O Great King, considering that they shall fulfill the equipment for enlightenment and, having attained the threefold enlightenment in due order, achieve final liberation— this is the well-spoken word of the Blessed One."
"Listening yourself, you should always cause the people to hear [the teaching] with reverence.
Having heard this instruction from the Arhat, King Aśoka joyfully bowed to that Arhat ascetic and, with palms joined in reverence, questioned him thus: (977–978)

What meritorious deed was performed by Maṇicūḍa in the past, by which he became a king, a ruler of men, and a sovereign of all the world? And how did that great jewel come to be born upon his head? (979)
And when he was born, divine jewels rained down;
celestial banners and flags were raised in the sky by the gods,
and divine musical instruments were struck on all sides.

A celestial jewel-encrusted parasol was held aloft in the sky by the gods, and throughout all the worlds, auspicious enthusiasm was set in motion; indeed, the ten directions were pervaded everywhere by his fame. 982.
The Bodhisattva was also known as Sarvadada, the Great Giver; furthermore, a great jewel appeared upon his crown—having explained all of this, awaken us all. 983–984.
When the lord of men had thus questioned him,
that Sanmati Upagupta, looking toward the king, spoke as follows:
"Listen well, O Great King, to what was done by Maṇicūḍa."
I shall briefly relate to you all that was well-performed in the past.
Long ago, there appeared a Tathāgata named Śikhin,
a perfectly enlightened Buddha, a Blessed One, an Arhat, a King of Dharma, and a Lord of Sages.
That omniscient Lord of the World, having taught the True Dharma throughout all worlds, practiced for the welfare of the world;
then that Blessed One went to the great city of Aruṇavatī.
Having taken up residence there, he taught the Dharma and dwelt together with his community of monks (saṃgha).
In that delightful great park, within the monastery, he remained teaching the Dharma after having acted for the benefit of all sentient beings, together with his disciples (śrāvakas). 989–990.
Thus, having brought about the world consisting of all dharmas and completed the work of a Sugata, that Blessed One attained supreme nirvāṇa.
Seeing that, King Aruṇa [honored] the body of the Teacher according to the prescribed rites.
Having consecrated the bones according to the ritual, he gathered them and purified them thoroughly.
That lord of the earth, having enshrined those bones within the inner sanctum,
constructed a magnificent stupa made of jewels.
Then that king, the ruler of men, having joyfully consecrated that stūpa according to the prescribed rites, attended upon it with great enthusiasm;
thus did that monarch act, bringing all the people dependent upon him under its influence.
Having established that great festival as well, he constantly maintained high enthusiasm;
thus that king, the ruler, together with his ministers, country-folk, and citizens, always honored it with great zeal, remaining devoted to that stūpa. (995–996)
Then, after some time, that king, having grown old and become extremely decrepit,
remembered that Sugata, cast off his body, and went to Sukhāvatī;
and those who had relied upon him also worshipped him with joy at all times.
They all, at that time, having cast off their bodies, went to Sukhāvatī.
(998) Thereafter, after some time, that stūpa became old and dilapidated;
struck by rain and wind, it was broken, collapsed, and split apart. (999)

Seeing that stūpa in ruins, the king, the son of Aruṇa, recalled the majesty of the qualities of the Triple Gem and reflected thus: "Alas, alas! This stūpa, the abode of the Victors of the Dharmadhātu, has fallen into decay. (1000)

The repository of the virtues and glory of the True Dharma, the bearer of the jewel of the wisdom of perfect enlightenment— (1001) for if this stūpa is broken, even the enthusiasm of sentient beings who possess faith and devotion for worship will become shattered and ruined. (1002)
Having restored it and established it according to the ritual,
I shall cause it to be beautifully adorned with banners, parasols, and flags; then all the people, seeing it thus well-adorned, [will rejoice].
Filled with great enthusiasm, they would attend upon him with joy. Then all those people, having purified the three spheres,
would become practitioners of the path to enlightenment, upholding the true qualities of the glory of the Dharma.
Then those pure-souled ones, free from afflictions and practicing celibacy,
having attained the threefold awakening as Arhats, went to perfect nirvāṇa; reflecting thus, the king, longing for the virtues of the True Dharma, [acted accordingly].

Having restored that stūpa, he caused it to be beautifully adorned. There, the joyful king, having plucked out his own crest-jewel (cūḍāmaṇi) and placed it upon the circle of the uṣṇīṣa of that stūpa, decorated it most magnificently.
Having adorned it with umbrellas, banners, and flags, with celestial garments and ornaments,
and with garlands of jasmine flowers, he made it exceedingly beautiful;
having installed it with great enthusiasm and worshipped it joyfully according to the prescribed rite.
Having brought all the musical instruments into harmony, they celebrated a great festival; lighting rows of lamps kindled with fragrant oil,
he placed upon his own head a lamp burning with the five kinds of clarified butter.
Having honored him with lotuses and performed circumambulations,
and having prostrated with the eight limbs, he joyfully made this aspiration:
"May I too, having attained such qualities of Dharma, work for the welfare of the world."
"Having attained perfect enlightenment, may I proceed to complete nirvāṇa. Having thus maintained this vow, that king, the son of Aruṇa,
always worshipped that stūpa with great enthusiasm and joy.
Having thus performed his devotions, he lived happily for a very long time; finally, maintaining mindfulness of the Buddha, he departed for the abode of the Jina.
He who was that king, the great being, the lord of the earth, the son of Aruṇa—1015.
This very Maṇicūḍa was once that sovereign of kings;
because he restored the stūpa of the Teacher Śikhin, by that merit he became a lord of the world, a king who bestowed both Dharma and wealth.
And because he had offered that great parasol upon that stūpa,
through the ripening of that merit, in his birth there appeared a beautiful divine parasol made of jewels and yak-tail fans in the sky.
Because he was sustained by serene deities above him,
and because he honored the stūpa with banners and flags,
for that reason, when he was born, those banners and flags were raised up by the gods.
And because that crest-jewel was placed upon his uṣṇīṣa, a jewel endowed with infinite qualities was produced upon his head;
and because a lamp kindled with the five kinds of ghee was borne upon his crown.
He gave him twice that amount, more magnificent, and that very jewel.
(1022) Thus, that Great Being, having taken refuge in this stūpa and established a great festival, always worshipped it with intense devotion. (1023)
Having likewise caused all the worlds to take refuge in the stūpas, he always inspired them with great enthusiasm and respect.
By the power of this merit, he attained the sovereign majesty over all the worlds.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva was endowed with the virtues of auspicious glory.
Furthermore, in the past, that Mahāsattva was Maṇicūḍa,
a most steadfast caravan leader who bore the welfare of all sentient beings in mind.
Then, at one time, having taken jewels from the ocean, he set out with his caravans; traveling with great enthusiasm, he went into the midst of the forest.
There, in a certain forest tract, [he saw] one who was resting at the foot of a tree.
He saw a solitary buddha who had been freed from poison.
Upon seeing him, that lord of merchants approached him suddenly;
with palms joined in reverence, he bowed down and asked this with great respect: 1028–1029.
"Venerable sir, what illness or suffering arises in your body that I should wish to alleviate? Instruct me on that.
Having heard what was said by him, that Pratyekabuddha replied:
Having beheld that caravan leader, he gently commanded him thus:
"O virtuous caravan master, a snake has bitten my toe;
its venom now stings throughout my entire body as it spreads through me."
Having heard what was thus instructed by that Arhat, the wise man smeared him with medicinal herbs and suddenly restored him to health.
Then that Pratyekabuddha, having recovered and being filled with faith, [departed].
Beholding that caravan leader, she gladdened him with auspicious blessings.
Then that caravan leader, having bowed to the Sugata who was thus inspired with faith, made this aspiration with joined palms and joy.
Since I have anointed this Lord of Sages, whose body was afflicted by poison, with medicinal herbs and restored him to health,
I have become gracious through this merit in all my births. (1036)
May I become the healer of the diseases of all sentient beings. And by the merit of this water used for washing my body,
may those who are touched by it be free from illness, well-nourished, and possess pure faculties.
Having made this vow, that caravan leader bowed to each of those Sugatas and departed from there filled with joy;
then, that leader of the caravan traveled on happily together with the guild of merchants.
Having reached the city in haste, he arrived at his own home;
having entered that residence, he exchanged words of greeting with his kinsmen, relatives, and friends, and displayed great joy.
Then, endowed with the glory and qualities of great sovereignty and prosperity,
he always lived in happiness, giving to all supplicants according to their desires;
thus, having brought benefit to all sentient beings, he was filled with joy.
Having made offerings to the Three Jewels, he remained for a long time practicing virtue.
Then, at the time of death, with his mind mindful of the Three Jewels,
he cast off his body and, remaining in meditative absorption, departed for the abode of the Thirty-three Gods.
There too, that Great Being, awakening all the gods and honoring the Three Jewels, always moved about in auspiciousness.
Then, at that time, he passed away from there in order to bring benefit to the surface of the earth.
Having attained birth as a kṣatriya, he became King Maṇicūḍa.
Indeed, that very Maṇicūḍa, the lord of merchants and ruler of men, has now become this Teacher, Śākyamuni himself. (1046–1047)
Thus, in former incalculable births, that Blessed One, the Teacher,
was born into royal families and, after passing away, became the sovereign of all worlds.
Even then, in all those births, he was a Great Being.
With a mind set on perfect enlightenment, he gave to all who desired things according to their wishes.
Thus, throughout thousands of incalculable births, he always performed most difficult deeds while maintaining a mind set on enlightenment.
Through the ripening of this merit, even in this degenerate age, that Bodhisattva, having conquered all the hosts of Māra, became free from afflictions with stainless faculties;
having attained Arhatship and perfect enlightenment, he became a fully awakened Lord of Sages. 1051
Then that Blessed One, the Teacher, awakening all sentient beings and establishing them on the path to enlightenment, constantly caused them to dwell in perfect auspiciousness;
thus did that Lord of the Three Worlds make the world consist of the Dharma.
Having completed his work for the sake of the Sugatas, he attained perfect peace.
(1053) Thus, this well-spoken account of the Teacher of the World’s accomplishment of the Dharma of Enlightenment should be joyfully heard by beings who desire awakening. (1054)

For those who, with reverence, faith, and devotion, listen with great care to this sublime discourse on the conduct of enlightenment spoken by that Blessed One— all of them become pure-souled, becoming the locus of auspicious glory and excellent virtues. (1055)
May the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, who dwell in the four Brahma-abodes,
having maintained the vow for perfect enlightenment and taken refuge in the Three Jewels,
and having undertaken the discipline of the Bodhisattva conduct, act for the welfare of the world.
Then all those noble ones, having purified the three spheres,
should always practice with enthusiasm for accomplishing the true Dharma throughout existence;
thus, having fully accomplished all the perfections in their proper sequence.
Having established goodness everywhere, they should move about with concentrated minds.
Then, all those practitioners of the holy life, being free from afflictions, shall become Arhats;
having conquered all the hosts of Māra, they shall fully attain perfect enlightenment.
Then all those Sugatas, the Kings of Dharma and Lords of Sages,
having fully taught the True Dharma, shall awaken the people of the world.
Then, in the three worlds, they [shall establish] the accomplishment of the qualities of the True Dharma.
Having established them on the path to enlightenment, they would cause them to practice for the welfare of the world.
Thus, all those Buddhas, having made the world consist of Dharma and having completed all their tasks, proceeded to perfect nirvana.
"This is the truth proclaimed by all the lords of sages"—
this was instructed to me by my teacher, and having heard it, I speak thus. Having thus reflected upon the well-spoken *Bodhicaryāvatāra* of the Teacher of the World, 1064.

Having heard this yourself, you ought to cause all people to hear it as well. (1065) In this way, may there always be welfare for you, may misfortune certainly cease, may there never be a journey to an evil rebirth, and may there always be movement toward a happy state. (1066)
Having always enjoyed virtuous enthusiasm and being a refuge for the excellent qualities of glory, one should maintain mindfulness of the Three Jewels and, at the end, go to the abode of the Jina;
having understood this truth and heard this well-spoken verse. (1067)
Performing service to the Three Jewels, practice the vow of the conduct of awakening.
Knowing that whatever karma has been committed must inevitably bear its fruit, one should always perform virtuous deeds within saṃsāra. (1068–1069)

For actions do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons; having reached the necessary conditions and the proper time, they bear fruit within the six realms of existence. (1070) Action is not burned by fire, nor is it moistened by water.
It is not dried up by the winds, nor does it perish upon the earth.
(1071) For in the ripening of white karma, there is always only whiteness;
but in the ripening of black karma, there is always only blackness.

"O King of Kings, understanding that even when the ripening of karma is mixed, the resulting fruit is indeed mixed (verse 1072), one should strive with diligence to abandon all black karmas, even those that are mixed with others (verse 1073)."
"Those who desire welfare should always exert great energy and effort in deeds that are exclusively auspicious and lead to enlightenment.
Having heard this instruction from the Arhat, King Aśoka was filled with joy.
Having thus given his promise, Satyaka rejoiced. Those who,
delighting in the virtues of the Sugata, hear this Avadāna of Maṇicūḍa with joy,
and those who, with faith and clarity, cause it to be heard with diligent and delighted minds— [for them there is great merit].

Those who, gladdened by the virtues of the Jina, speak with devotion, desiring the Bodhi and the true Dharma—they are all Bodhisattvas who have gone for refuge to the Triple Gem and are liberated from the conduct of Māra;
they are enriched with the excellent qualities of auspicious glory, possess utterly pure minds, and are intent on the welfare of all sentient beings. 1076.

Having constantly performed virtuous deeds, being devoted to the Dharma King who is free from the three stains, maintaining the conduct of awakening, and possessing all excellent qualities, they become sovereign lords of all phenomena; having enjoyed the auspicious bliss of glory, they finally attain supreme joy in the abode of the One Possessing the Ten Powers. 1077
Thus ends the noble avadāna of the Bodhisattva, the Great King Maṇicūḍa, the Mahāsattva, in the glorious Mahājātakamālā.
